The catalog provides lineage tracking, glossary terms, and a searchable inventory of all organizational data assets. This is the data governance component of Microsoft Purview.
DLP prevents sensitive data from being shared inappropriately. It doesn't discover and catalogue data assets across multiple cloud platforms.
eDiscovery searches for content within Microsoft 365 (Exchange, SharePoint, Teams) for legal purposes. It doesn't scan Azure databases, blob storage, or third-party cloud services.
questions.tip: Microsoft Purview data governance: Data Map → scan data sources, create asset inventory. Data Catalog → searchable catalog of all discovered assets. Data Estate Insights → analytics on data estate. Supported sources: Azure (SQL, Blob, ADLS, Synapse), on-premises (SQL Server, Oracle, SAP), multi-cloud (AWS S3, Glue, RDS), SaaS (Power BI, M365). Classification: automatic sensitive info type detection during scanning. Lineage: visual data flow from source to destination.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization has Windows 365 Cloud PCs and physical Windows devices
- Some users have both a Cloud PC and a physical laptop
- The IT team wants the same Intune policies, apps, and configurations to apply to both the Cloud PC and the physical device
- Users should have a consistent experience regardless of which device they use

Question:
How does Intune manage Windows 365 Cloud PCs compared to physical devices?
choices: Cloud PCs require a separate Intune tenant and separate policies
Cloud PCs are managed the same way as physical devices in Intune — same policies, profiles, and apps can target both
Cloud PCs cannot be managed by Intune — they use a separate management tool
Cloud PCs only support a subset of Intune policies and cannot receive app deployments
explanations: Cloud PCs and physical devices are managed in the same Intune tenant. There's no need for a separate tenant or separate policies.

This option is correct. Windows 365 Cloud PCs appear in Intune as regular Windows devices. They can receive the same device configuration profiles, compliance policies, security baselines, app deployments, and endpoint security settings as physical devices. You can target the same device groups with the same policies, ensuring a consistent management experience. Cloud PCs also support Windows Update management, BitLocker, and Defender for Endpoint.
Cloud PCs are fully managed through Intune. They automatically enrol in Intune during provisioning and appear alongside physical devices in the device inventory.
Cloud PCs support the full range of Intune policies and app deployments. There's no limitation compared to physical devices for standard management scenarios.
questions.tip: Windows 365 + Intune: Cloud PCs auto-enrol in Intune during provisioning. Same policies as physical devices: configuration profiles, compliance, security baselines, apps. Cloud PC-specific features: resize (change specs), reprovision (fresh Cloud PC), point-in-time restore. Management parity: almost identical to physical Windows device management. Best practice: use the same Azure AD groups for both Cloud PCs and physical devices when policies should be consistent.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization has Microsoft 365 E5
- The legal team creates a sensitivity label called 'Legal Privileged'
- This label applies AES-256 encryption, restricts access to the Legal department Azure AD group, and adds a 'Legal Privileged — Do Not Distribute' watermark
- A user from the Marketing department receives a document with this label

Question:
What happens when the Marketing user tries to open the document?
choices: The document opens normally without any restrictions
The Marketing user is blocked from opening the document because they are not in the Legal department group
The document opens but without the watermark
The sensitivity label is automatically removed and the document opens unprotected
explanations: The label's encryption restricts access to the Legal department group only. Users outside this group cannot decrypt the document, so it will not open normally.

This option is correct. When a sensitivity label applies encryption with specific group permissions, only members of the authorized groups can open the document. The Marketing user is not in the Legal department Azure AD group, so the encryption prevents them from decrypting and opening the document. They will see a message indicating they don't have permission to access the file. The protection travels with the document — it doesn't matter where the file is stored or how it was shared.
Watermarks are embedded in the document along with the encryption. You can't have one without the other — if the document can't be opened, neither the content nor the watermark is visible.

Sensitivity labels with encryption persist. The label and protection cannot be removed by unauthorised users. Only users with the proper rights (typically the label administrator or content owner) can change or remove labels.
questions.tip: Sensitivity label encryption behavior: Authorized users → full access per assigned permissions (view, edit, print). Unauthorized users → cannot open/decrypt the document at all. Protection persistence: encryption stays regardless of file location (email, USB, cloud storage). Owner rights: document owner/creator typically retains full control. Super user: designated admins can access all encrypted content for compliance/legal purposes. Authentication: users authenticate via Azure AD to verify group membership before decryption.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization uses Intune to manage Android Enterprise devices
- The IT team needs to deploy apps to corporate-owned fully managed Android devices
- The apps should be sourced from the Google Play Store but managed through Intune
- Users should not have access to the full public Google Play Store — only approved apps should be visible

Question:
How should you deploy managed apps to Android Enterprise fully managed devices?
choices: Allow users full access to the public Google Play Store
Approve apps in Managed Google Play and deploy through Intune as Required or Available
Sideload APK files manually on each device
Deploy apps through a third-party app store
explanations: Full Google Play Store access on corporate devices allows users to install any app, including potentially insecure or distracting apps. Corporate-owned devices should restrict app availability to IT-approved apps.

This option is correct. Managed Google Play is the enterprise version of Google Play integrated with Intune. The IT admin approves specific apps in Managed Google Play, and only approved apps are visible to users on their managed devices. Apps are assigned through Intune as Required (auto-install) or Available (user-initiated from managed Play Store). This provides a curated app catalogue for corporate devices.
Manual APK sideloading bypasses app management, doesn't provide update management, and requires physical access or complex deployment scripts. It's not the enterprise approach.
Third-party app stores are not supported in Android Enterprise management. Managed Google Play is the integrated solution for Android Enterprise devices.
questions.tip: Managed Google Play: Approve apps → admin selects which apps are available. Deploy via Intune: Required (auto-install), Available (user installs from Managed Play). Web apps: create web app links in Managed Google Play. Private apps: upload private APKs to Managed Google Play for internal distribution. User experience: Managed Play Store shows only approved apps. Auto-update: managed apps auto-update from Managed Play. No personal Google account needed on fully managed/dedicated devices.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization has 100 devices enrolled in Intune
- A critical compliance policy requires all devices to have antivirus real-time protection enabled
- The compliance policy marks devices as non-compliant if real-time protection is disabled
- A Conditional Access policy blocks non-compliant devices from accessing Microsoft 365
- A user intentionally disables Windows Defender real-time protection

Question:
What sequence of events occurs after the user disables real-time protection?
choices: The device is immediately blocked from Microsoft 365 within seconds
At the next Intune compliance check, the device is marked non-compliant; Conditional Access then blocks Microsoft 365 access on the next sign-in or token refresh
Nothing happens — Intune cannot detect antivirus settings
The user receives an email warning but access is never blocked
explanations: The block is not immediate. Compliance evaluation happens during scheduled check-ins (typically every 8 hours for Windows), not in real-time. There's a delay between the configuration change and the access block.

This option is correct. The sequence is: 1) User disables real-time protection. 2) At the next compliance evaluation (scheduled check-in, typically every 8 hours), Intune evaluates the compliance policy. 3) The device is marked non-compliant. 4) On the next sign-in or token refresh, Conditional Access evaluates the device's compliance state and blocks access to Microsoft 365. The delay between disabling protection and losing access depends on the check-in schedule and token lifetime.
Intune can detect Windows Defender antivirus settings including real-time protection status. This is a standard compliance policy setting.

If Conditional Access is configured to require device compliance, access IS blocked — it's not just a warning. Non-compliance actions can include email warnings as an additional action, but the CA policy enforces the block.
questions.tip: Compliance evaluation timeline: 1. Configuration change on device. 2. Next scheduled compliance check (every 8h for Windows). 3. Device marked non-compliant. 4. Conditional Access blocks on next token evaluation. Speed up: manual sync triggers immediate re-evaluation. Continuous access evaluation (CAE): can speed up enforcement for supported apps. Non-compliance actions timeline: immediately → mark non-compliant. After grace period → send notification. After deadline → block access, wipe device, etc.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization uses Microsoft 365 with Conditional Access
- The security team identifies that legacy authentication protocols (POP3, IMAP, SMTP AUTH) are being used by some users
- These protocols do not support MFA and are commonly exploited in password spray attacks
- The team wants to block all legacy authentication while allowing modern authentication

Question:
How should you block legacy authentication?
choices: Disable POP3 and IMAP in Exchange Online for each mailbox individually
Create a Conditional Access policy that blocks access when the client app condition is 'Other clients' (legacy authentication)
Remove all user passwords and require certificate-based authentication
Block port 110 (POP3) and port 143 (IMAP) on the corporate firewall
explanations: Disabling protocols per mailbox is time-consuming for large organizations and doesn't cover SMTP AUTH or Exchange ActiveSync (older versions). A Conditional Access policy provides a centralized, scalable solution.

This option is correct. Conditional Access has a 'Client apps' condition that includes 'Other clients' (legacy authentication protocols). Create a policy: All users (exclude break-glass accounts) → All cloud apps → Client apps = Other clients (legacy authentication) → Block access. This blocks POP3, IMAP, SMTP AUTH, and older Exchange ActiveSync from authenticating, while modern authentication (OAuth 2.0) continues to work normally.

Removing passwords and requiring certificates is extremely disruptive and may not be feasible for many organizations. Certificate-based authentication requires PKI infrastructure and is a major implementation effort.

Blocking ports at the firewall only affects traffic from the corporate network. Users connecting from home, public Wi-Fi, or mobile networks bypass the corporate firewall entirely. Conditional Access blocks at the identity layer regardless of network path.
questions.tip: Legacy authentication blocking: Conditional Access → Client apps → 'Other clients' → Block. Legacy protocols blocked: POP3, IMAP, SMTP AUTH, older EAS, MAPI, EWS (basic auth), Remote PowerShell (basic auth). Modern auth not affected: OAuth 2.0, ADAL, MSAL. Deployment: 1. Report-only mode first. 2. Check sign-in logs for legacy auth usage. 3. Migrate users/apps to modern auth. 4. Enable enforcement. Important: some line-of-business apps may still use legacy auth — identify them before blocking.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your company is migrating from Group Policy (GPO) to Intune for device management
- The IT team has hundreds of existing GPO settings that need to be replicated in Intune
- They need a tool to analyze existing GPOs and determine which settings can be configured in Intune

Question:
Which Microsoft tool helps analyze existing GPOs for Intune migration?
explanations: Azure AD Connect synchronizes on-premises AD identities to Azure AD. It doesn't analyze Group Policy settings or assist with GPO-to-Intune migration.

This option is correct. Group Policy analytics in Intune allows you to import existing GPO backups (XML) and analyze them. For each GPO setting, it shows: whether the setting is supported in Intune (via MDM, Settings Catalog, or ADMX templates), whether there's a matching Intune setting, and which settings have no Intune equivalent. This helps IT teams plan their migration and identify gaps before starting the transition.
The Assessment and Planning Toolkit evaluates infrastructure readiness for migrations (like cloud migration readiness) but doesn't specifically analyze GPO settings for Intune compatibility.
SCCM (MECM) is a device management platform that works alongside GPO. It doesn't analyze GPO settings for Intune migration.
questions.tip: GPO to Intune migration: 1. Export GPO backups (PowerShell: Backup-GPO). 2. Import to Intune → Devices → Group Policy analytics. 3. Review analysis: MDM support status per setting. 4. Create Intune profiles for supported settings. Setting support levels: MDM Supported (full equivalent in Intune), ADMX Supported (use ADMX templates), Not Supported (no Intune equivalent). For unsupported settings: consider custom OMA-URI, PowerShell scripts, or accepting the gap.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization uses Microsoft Purview
- The HR department uploads employee performance reviews to a SharePoint document library
- Each review contains the employee's full name, employee ID, and performance rating
- The compliance team wants to automatically detect and protect documents containing employee performance data

Question:
Which approach should you use to detect employee performance review documents?
choices: Create a custom sensitive information type that matches the document pattern (employee ID format + performance-related keywords)
Manually review every document uploaded to the SharePoint library
Block all uploads to the SharePoint library
Encrypt the entire SharePoint site with a sensitivity label
explanations: This option is correct. Create a custom sensitive information type in Microsoft Purview that uses a combination of: a regex pattern matching your employee ID format (e.g., 'EMP-\d{6}'), keywords related to performance reviews ('performance rating', 'annual review', 'objective assessment'), and optionally corroborative evidence (employee names from a keyword dictionary). This SIT can then be used in DLP policies to detect and protect performance review documents, and in auto-labeling policies to automatically apply sensitivity labels.
Manual review doesn't scale and is prone to human error. With hundreds or thousands of documents, automated detection is the only practical approach.
Blocking all uploads prevents the HR department from using SharePoint for its intended purpose. The requirement is to detect and protect specific content, not block all content.

Encrypting the entire site with a sensitivity label protects all documents equally, even non-sensitive ones. It doesn't provide targeted detection of performance review documents and may over-restrict access to non-sensitive content.
questions.tip: Custom sensitive information types: Pattern elements: regex (custom format matching), keyword lists (contextual terms), keyword dictionaries (large lists), functions (Luhn checksum, date validation). Confidence levels: low (regex match), medium (+ keywords), high (+ corroborative evidence). Use in: DLP policies, auto-labeling, retention policies, eDiscovery. Test: use the 'Test' function in Purview to validate against sample documents before deployment. Alternative: trainable classifiers for document types that are hard to define by pattern.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization has 1,000 Windows devices managed by Intune
- The IT team needs to ensure all devices have the latest quality updates installed within 5 days of release
- If a device hasn't installed the update after 5 days, it should be forced to restart and install
- Users should receive notifications before any forced restart

Question:
Which Intune feature enforces this update installation deadline?
choices: Windows Update ring with deadline settings
Device compliance policy requiring latest updates
explanations: Feature update profiles control Windows version upgrades (e.g., Windows 10 to 11), not monthly quality/security updates.

This option is correct. Windows Update rings in Intune include deadline settings that force update installation after a specified number of days. Configure: quality update deferral period, deadline (5 days), grace period, and user notification settings. After the deadline, Windows automatically installs the update and restarts the device. Users receive notifications before the forced restart, giving them time to save work.
Compliance policies can check if updates are installed but don't force installation or manage restart deadlines. They evaluate state, not enforce updates.
Expedite policies bypass deferrals for emergency patches. They're for urgent out-of-band updates, not for routine deadline enforcement on regular quality updates.
questions.tip: Update ring deadline settings: Deadline for quality updates → days before forced install. Deadline for feature updates → days before forced install. Grace period → additional hours after deadline before restart. Auto-reboot before deadline → yes/no. Notification: users see countdown reminders as deadline approaches. Engaged restart: additional prominent notifications in final hours.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization uses Microsoft Purview
- The compliance team needs to automatically apply retention rules to emails based on content
- Emails containing the phrase 'contract agreement' should be retained for 7 years
- Emails without this phrase should follow the default 2-year retention
- The retention labels must be applied automatically without user action

Question:
How should you implement content-based retention?
choices: Create a mail flow rule that tags emails containing 'contract agreement'
Create a retention label with 7-year retention and auto-apply it using a keyword query policy
Create a DLP policy that retains emails matching the keyword
Ask users to manually apply retention labels to contract emails
explanations: Mail flow rules can tag or categorize emails but cannot apply retention labels. Retention is managed through Microsoft Purview, not Exchange mail flow rules.

This option is correct. Create a retention label configured with a 7-year retain-then-delete action. Then create an auto-apply label policy using a keyword query condition (KQL: 'contract agreement'). The policy scans Exchange content and automatically applies the retention label to matching emails. A separate org-wide retention policy handles the default 2-year retention for all other emails.
DLP policies prevent data sharing but don't manage retention or apply retention labels. DLP and retention are separate compliance features.
Manual label application depends on users remembering to label every contract email, which is unreliable. The requirement specifies automatic application without user action.
questions.tip: Auto-apply retention labels: Conditions: keyword query (KQL), sensitive info types, trainable classifiers. Locations: Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive. Processing: scans existing and new content. Priority: auto-applied labels don't override manually applied labels. Combined with org-wide retention policy: auto-label for specific content + blanket policy for everything else. KQL examples: 'contract agreement', 'subject:invoice', 'from:legal@company.com'.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization uses Intune to manage Windows devices
- The IT team deploys a Win32 app with the following detection rule: file C:\Program Files\AppX\app.exe exists with version >= 3.0
- After deployment, Intune reports the app as 'Not installed' on devices that actually have it installed
- Investigation reveals the app installs to C:\Program Files (x86)\AppX\app.exe on 64-bit systems

Question:
What is causing the detection rule to fail?
choices: The detection rule file path doesn't match the actual installation path — the app installs to Program Files (x86), not Program Files
Intune cannot detect Win32 apps on 64-bit systems
The detection rule needs to use a registry key instead of a file path
explanations: Even if the version were below 3.0, the issue is the path mismatch. The detection rule looks in 'Program Files' but the app installs to 'Program Files (x86)'. The file wouldn't be found at the specified path regardless of version.

This option is correct. The detection rule specifies C:\Program Files\AppX\app.exe, but the 32-bit application installs to C:\Program Files (x86)\AppX\app.exe on 64-bit Windows. Intune looks at the exact path specified in the detection rule. Since no file exists at the specified path, the detection fails and Intune reports 'Not installed'. Fix: update the detection rule path to C:\Program Files (x86)\AppX\app.exe, or check the 'associated with a 32-bit app on 64-bit clients' checkbox.
Intune fully supports Win32 app detection on 64-bit systems. The issue is the path mismatch, not a platform limitation.
While registry-based detection is an alternative, it's not required. File-based detection works perfectly when the path is correct. The issue is the incorrect file path, not the detection method.
questions.tip: Win32 app detection rules — common issues: Wrong path: Program Files vs Program Files (x86). 32-bit app checkbox: enables checking the 32-bit registry/file system on 64-bit OS. Version comparison: ensure version format matches (1.0 vs 1.0.0.0). Registry detection: HKLM vs HKCU, correct key path. Best practice: test detection rule manually on a target device before deploying. Three detection types: File (path + version/date/size), Registry (key + value), MSI (product code + version).

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization has Azure AD Premium P1
- The IT team needs to automate user provisioning to third-party SaaS applications (Salesforce, ServiceNow, Zoom)
- When a user is created in Azure AD, their account should be automatically created in these SaaS apps
- When a user is disabled in Azure AD, their SaaS app accounts should be deprovisioned

Question:
Which Azure AD feature automates user lifecycle management for SaaS applications?
choices: Azure AD automatic user provisioning (SCIM-based provisioning)
explanations: Azure AD Connect synchronises identities between on-premises AD and Azure AD. It doesn't provision user accounts into third-party SaaS applications like Salesforce or ServiceNow.

This option is correct. Azure AD automatic user provisioning uses the SCIM (System for Cross-domain Identity Management) protocol to automatically create, update, and delete user accounts in third-party SaaS applications. When configured, user creation/modification/deletion in Azure AD triggers corresponding actions in the connected SaaS apps. This provides automated user lifecycle management across your SaaS ecosystem.
Conditional Access controls access to apps based on conditions (device, location, risk) but doesn't create or manage user accounts within those applications.
Azure AD B2B enables external users (guests) to access your organization's resources. It doesn't provision internal user accounts into external SaaS applications.
questions.tip: Azure AD provisioning: Protocol: SCIM 2.0 (standard API for identity provisioning). Supported apps: thousands in Azure AD gallery (Salesforce, ServiceNow, Zoom, etc.). Provisioning modes: automatic (sync on schedule) or on-demand (test single user). Attribute mapping: map Azure AD attributes to SaaS app attributes. Scoping: provision all users or specific groups. Deprovisioning: disable or delete SaaS accounts when user is removed from scope.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization has Microsoft 365 E5
- The security team wants to enforce that only FIDO2 security keys can be used for MFA when accessing highly sensitive applications
- Standard MFA methods (phone, authenticator app) should NOT be accepted for these applications
- Other applications can continue using any MFA method

Question:
Which Conditional Access feature restricts authentication to specific strong methods?
choices: Authentication strength (built-in or custom authentication strength policy)
explanations: Standard 'Require MFA' accepts any registered MFA method (phone call, SMS, authenticator app push, FIDO2, Windows Hello). It doesn't restrict which specific MFA method must be used.

This option is correct. Authentication strength in Conditional Access allows you to define which authentication methods are acceptable for specific scenarios. Built-in strengths include: MFA strength (any MFA), Passwordless MFA strength (Windows Hello, FIDO2, certificate), Phishing-resistant MFA strength (FIDO2, Windows Hello, certificate). You can also create custom authentication strengths specifying exactly which methods are allowed (e.g., FIDO2 security keys only). Apply different strengths to different Conditional Access policies targeting different apps.
Require approved client app limits which applications can access services but doesn't control authentication methods. It's about the app identity, not the authentication strength.
Sign-in frequency controls how often users must re-authenticate but doesn't specify which authentication methods they must use.
questions.tip: Authentication strength levels: MFA → any MFA method. Passwordless MFA → Windows Hello, FIDO2, certificate-based auth. Phishing-resistant MFA → FIDO2, Windows Hello, certificate (no phone-based methods). Custom → pick specific methods. Use case: sensitive apps → phishing-resistant only. General apps → any MFA. Conditional Access: select authentication strength in grant controls instead of 'Require MFA'. Requires: Azure AD Premium P1+.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization manages Windows devices with Intune
- The IT team wants to monitor device startup performance
- They need to identify devices with slow boot times and determine the root cause
- Metrics should include: total boot time, time to desktop, and impact of Group Policy processing

Question:
Which Intune feature provides device startup performance analytics?
choices: Microsoft Defender for Endpoint device health
explanations: Device compliance reports show whether devices meet compliance policy requirements. They don't measure performance metrics like boot time.

This option is correct. Endpoint Analytics in Intune includes a Startup performance section that measures: total boot time, time to desktop, Group Policy processing time, core boot time, and sign-in time. It identifies devices with slow startups and highlights the contributing factors (slow disk, too many startup apps, lengthy GPO processing). IT teams can use this data to optimise the user experience and identify hardware or software issues affecting boot performance.
Windows Update compliance reports show update installation status, not device performance metrics.
Defender for Endpoint device health monitors security-related health (sensor status, antivirus status) not boot performance.
questions.tip: Endpoint Analytics sections: Startup performance → boot time, sign-in time, GP processing. Application reliability → app crash rates, hang rates. Proactive remediations → detect/fix issues automatically. Resource performance → CPU, memory, disk usage. Startup performance insights: total boot time breakdown, top processes impacting startup, devices with degrading performance, model-based comparison. Requirements: Windows 10/11, Intune enrolled or co-managed.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization uses Microsoft Defender for Endpoint
- A new zero-day vulnerability is announced affecting a widely-used application
- No patch is available yet from the vendor
- The security team needs to reduce risk by blocking the vulnerable application from running until a patch is released

Question:
Which Defender for Endpoint feature can block a specific application from executing?
choices: Indicators of compromise (IoC) — file hash block
explanations: Web content filtering blocks access to websites by category. It doesn't control application execution on endpoints.

This option is correct. Indicators of compromise (IoC) in Defender for Endpoint allow you to create file indicators using the application's file hash (SHA-256). When set to 'Block and remediate', Defender prevents the file from executing on all onboarded devices. This effectively blocks the vulnerable application until a patch is available. You can also use certificate-based indicators to block all versions signed by a specific certificate.
Network protection blocks connections to malicious domains/IPs. It doesn't prevent local application execution.
Controlled folder access protects specific folders from unauthorised changes (ransomware protection). It doesn't block application execution.
questions.tip: Defender for Endpoint blocking mechanisms: File indicators (IoC) → block by file hash, certificate. Application control (WDAC) → whitelist-based application control. Attack surface reduction → block specific behaviors. Network indicators → block by IP, URL, domain. File indicator actions: Allow, Audit, Warn, Block, Block and remediate. Use IoC for quick emergency blocking. Use WDAC for long-term application control policy.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization manages iOS devices with Intune
- The IT team needs to purchase 500 licences for a paid iOS app and distribute them to specific users
- When a user leaves the company, the licence should be reclaimed and reassigned
- The app must be deployed silently without user action on supervised devices

Question:
Which approach should you use for this managed app deployment?
choices: Give each user a corporate credit card to purchase the app individually
Purchase device-based licences through Apple Business Manager VPP and deploy as Required via Intune
Deploy a web clip linking to the App Store page
Use Apple Configurator to install via USB on each device
explanations: Individual purchases tie licences to personal Apple IDs, making them unrecoverable when employees leave. This is not scalable and provides no central management.

This option is correct. Purchase licences through Apple Business Manager (VPP — Volume Purchase Program) and sync to Intune via VPP token. Use device-based licensing so no Apple ID is needed on the device. Assign as Required for silent deployment on supervised devices. When a user leaves, revoke the licence in Intune and it becomes available for reassignment. This is the enterprise-standard approach for paid iOS app deployment.
A web clip creates a shortcut to a URL, not an installed app. It cannot install paid apps or manage licences.
USB installation via Apple Configurator doesn't scale to 500 devices and doesn't provide licence management or reclamation.
questions.tip: VPP app licencing types: User-based → licence tied to user's Managed Apple ID, follows user across devices. Device-based → licence tied to device, no Apple ID needed, silent install. Device-based advantages: no Apple ID requirement, silent install on supervised devices, simpler user experience. Licence reclamation: revoke in Intune → licence returns to pool. VPP token: syncs ABM purchases to Intune, auto-renews licences.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your company has remote workers using personal Windows devices (BYOD)
- These devices are NOT enrolled in Intune MDM
- Workers need to access corporate SharePoint and OneDrive files
- The IT team wants to protect corporate data on these unmanaged devices without managing the entire device

Question:
Which approach protects corporate data on unenrolled Windows BYOD devices?
choices: Require device enrolment in Intune before allowing access
Use Windows MAM (Mobile Application Management without enrolment) with app protection policies for Windows
Allow unrestricted access with no protection
Block all BYOD access to corporate resources
explanations: Requiring MDM enrolment for personal devices is intrusive and many employees will object to IT having full device management over their personal computers.

This option is correct. Windows MAM (app protection policies without device enrolment) protects corporate data accessed through Microsoft Edge on unenrolled Windows devices. When users access corporate SharePoint/OneDrive through Edge, app protection policies enforce: data transfer restrictions (no copy/paste to personal apps), require PIN/biometric, encrypt org data, and selective wipe capability. The personal device remains unmanaged — only the corporate data within Edge is protected.
Unrestricted access on personal devices means corporate data has no protection. Users could freely copy, download, and share corporate files without any controls.
Blocking all BYOD access prevents remote workers from being productive. The business need is to enable access with appropriate protection, not block it entirely.
questions.tip: Windows MAM (without enrolment): Protects corporate data in Microsoft Edge on unmanaged Windows devices. Controls: cut/copy/paste restrictions, save-as restrictions, PIN required, encryption, selective wipe. User experience: sign into Edge with work account → policies automatically apply. No device enrolment needed. Conditional Access integration: require app protection policy for access. Supported: Windows 10/11, Microsoft Edge browser. Similar to: iOS/Android MAM without enrolment.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization uses Microsoft Purview
- The compliance team creates a DLP policy for Exchange Online
- The policy should detect emails containing more than 5 credit card numbers
- When detected, the email should be blocked and the sender should receive a notification explaining why
- The sender's manager should also be notified

Question:
Which DLP policy components should you configure?
choices: Condition: sensitive info type 'Credit Card Number' with instance count > 5; Action: block email; Notification: sender and sender's manager
Condition: keyword 'credit card'; Action: encrypt email; Notification: compliance team only
Condition: file size > 5 MB; Action: quarantine; Notification: sender only
Condition: external recipient; Action: add disclaimer; Notification: none
explanations: This option is correct. DLP policy configuration: Condition uses the built-in 'Credit Card Number' sensitive information type with an instance count threshold of 'more than 5' (meaning 6+ credit card numbers in one email). Action is set to 'Block the content' which prevents the email from being sent. User notifications are configured for the sender (explaining why the email was blocked with a policy tip) and the sender's manager (incident notification). This provides both enforcement and awareness.

Keyword matching for 'credit card' would generate false positives (any email discussing credit cards, even without actual numbers). The sensitive information type uses pattern matching with Luhn algorithm validation to detect real credit card numbers. Also, the requirement is to block, not encrypt.
File size has nothing to do with credit card number detection. This condition is completely unrelated to the requirement.
Checking for external recipients alone doesn't detect credit card numbers in the email content. The requirement is content-based detection, not recipient-based.
questions.tip: DLP policy components: Conditions → sensitive info types (pattern matching), instance count thresholds, confidence levels. Actions → block, encrypt, restrict access, add disclaimer. Notifications → policy tips (sender sees in Outlook), email notifications (sender, manager, compliance team). Instance count: 'more than 5' = trigger when 6+ instances found. Confidence levels: high (fewer false positives, may miss some), medium, low (more detections, more false positives). Override: optionally allow users to override the block with justification.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization has Intune-managed Windows devices
- The IT team needs to configure local administrator account management
- Requirements:
  - Each device should have a unique local admin password
  - Passwords should automatically rotate every 30 days
  - Admins should be able to retrieve the password from Azure AD/Intune

Question:
Which solution manages local admin passwords for Azure AD joined devices?
choices: Set the same local admin password on all devices via a PowerShell script
Windows LAPS (Local Administrator Password Solution) integrated with Azure AD
Disable the local admin account on all devices
Use Group Policy to set a common local admin password
explanations: Using the same password on all devices is a critical security risk. If one device is compromised, the attacker has admin access to every device. This approach has no rotation and no audit trail.

This option is correct. Windows LAPS (Local Administrator Password Solution) with Azure AD integration automatically generates unique, random local admin passwords for each device, stores them securely in Azure AD, rotates passwords on a configurable schedule (e.g., every 30 days), and allows authorized admins to retrieve passwords from the Azure AD portal or Intune. This provides secure local admin management for cloud-managed devices.
Disabling the local admin account removes a recovery mechanism. If Azure AD authentication fails or Intune connectivity is lost, there's no way to sign into the device locally for troubleshooting.
Group Policy can set a common password (via GPO Preferences) but this has the same vulnerability as option A — same password on all devices, compromising one compromises all.
questions.tip: Windows LAPS with Azure AD: Configure via Intune: Endpoint security → Account protection → LAPS. Settings: password complexity, length, rotation period, which local account to manage. Password storage: Azure AD device properties (encrypted). Password retrieval: Azure AD portal, Intune device details, Microsoft Graph API. Audit: all password retrievals are logged. Supports: Azure AD joined and hybrid Azure AD joined devices. Rotation: automatic on schedule + on-demand rotation available.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization uses Microsoft Teams
- Regulatory requirements mandate that certain departments (Investment Banking and Research) must NOT be able to communicate with each other via Teams
- Users within the same department should communicate freely
- All other departments should have no communication restrictions

Question:
Which Microsoft Purview feature prevents communication between these specific departments?
explanations: DLP policies detect sensitive content in Teams messages and can block sharing, but they don't prevent communication between specific groups of users regardless of content.

This option is correct. Information barriers in Microsoft Purview create bidirectional blocks between specified user segments. When configured, users in Investment Banking and Research cannot: find each other in Teams search, start chats or calls with each other, be added to the same Teams group chats or channels. Within-department communication is unaffected, and all other departments are unrestricted.

Communication compliance monitors message content for policy violations but doesn't block communication between specific groups. It reviews content after it's sent, not prevents communication entirely.
Conditional Access controls how and when users access Teams but doesn't restrict which users can communicate with each other within Teams.
questions.tip: Information barriers: Define segments → user groups based on Azure AD attributes (department, group). Define policies → block or allow between segments. Effects in Teams: no chat, no calls, no group additions, no search visibility between blocked segments. Effects in SharePoint/OneDrive: no sharing between blocked segments. Use cases: financial regulatory compliance (Chinese walls), conflict of interest, merger segregation. Requirements: Microsoft 365 E5 or E5 Compliance.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your company uses Intune to deploy apps to Windows devices
- The IT team deploys a Win32 app called 'DataProcessor' version 2.0
- Later, version 3.0 is released with security fixes
- The IT team wants to ensure all devices running version 2.0 are automatically upgraded to 3.0
- Version 2.0 should be uninstalled before version 3.0 is installed

Question:
How should you handle this version upgrade in Intune?
choices: Delete the v2.0 app from Intune and create a new v3.0 app
Configure v3.0 to supersede v2.0 with 'uninstall previous version' option
Deploy v3.0 alongside v2.0 and hope users uninstall the old version
Create a PowerShell script to uninstall v2.0 and install v3.0
explanations: Deleting the v2.0 app removes the assignment, but doesn't automatically deploy v3.0 to the same devices. You'd need to create v3.0 and re-assign it, and v2.0 wouldn't be automatically uninstalled.

This option is correct. Win32 app supersedence in Intune creates a relationship where v3.0 replaces v2.0. Configure v3.0 as the superseding app with the 'Uninstall previous version' option enabled. Intune automatically uninstalls v2.0 and installs v3.0 on all devices that had v2.0. The supersedence relationship handles the complete upgrade lifecycle.
Running two versions side-by-side can cause conflicts and doesn't ensure v2.0 is removed. Relying on users to uninstall is unreliable.
PowerShell scripts lack the management features of Intune app supersedence: no detection rules, no retry logic, no status reporting, no compliance tracking.
questions.tip: App supersedence workflow: 1. Create v3.0 app in Intune. 2. In v3.0 properties → Supersedence tab → add v2.0. 3. Choose action: Update (install over) or Uninstall (remove old, install new). 4. Assign v3.0. 5. Intune handles the transition on each device. Supersedence chains: v3.0 supersedes v2.0 which superseded v1.0. Intune manages the entire chain. Detection: v3.0 detection rules determine success.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your company has 50 Windows devices used as point-of-sale (POS) terminals
- Each terminal runs a single POS application in full-screen mode
- The devices should automatically sign in without requiring a user to enter credentials
- No access to the Windows desktop, taskbar, or Start menu should be available

Question:
Which Intune configuration should you deploy for these POS terminals?
choices: Multi-app kiosk mode with a custom Start menu
Single-app kiosk mode with auto-logon configured
Standard device configuration with app restriction
explanations: Multi-app kiosk provides a restricted but multi-application experience. POS terminals need only one application and shouldn't present any app selection interface.

This option is correct. Single-app kiosk mode replaces the Windows shell with a single application running in full-screen. Combined with auto-logon (a kiosk account that signs in automatically at boot), the device powers on directly into the POS application without any user authentication. No desktop, taskbar, or Start menu is accessible. This is the standard configuration for POS, digital signage, and single-purpose devices.

Standard device configuration with app restrictions still provides a Windows desktop experience. Users could potentially access other system features even with restrictions. Kiosk mode provides a much more locked-down environment.
Windows 365 Cloud PCs are virtual desktops in the cloud. POS terminals need local app execution with reliable performance and no dependency on internet connectivity for the primary POS function.
questions.tip: Single-app kiosk setup: 1. Create auto-logon account (local or Azure AD). 2. Specify the kiosk app (UWP app ID or Win32 path). 3. Deploy via Intune device configuration → Kiosk. Auto-logon: device boots directly into the app, no sign-in screen. Supported app types: UWP (recommended), Win32 (specify shell launcher). Combine with: Autopilot self-deploying mode for initial provisioning. Security: kiosk user has minimal privileges, no access to system settings.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization has Microsoft 365 E5
- The security team wants to protect against Business Email Compromise (BEC) attacks
- Attackers are impersonating the CEO by using a similar display name in emails from external domains
- The team needs to detect and quarantine these impersonation attempts

Question:
Which Microsoft Defender for Office 365 feature protects against impersonation attacks?
explanations: Safe Attachments scans email attachments in a sandbox environment. It doesn't analyse sender display names or detect impersonation attempts.

This option is correct. Anti-phishing policies in Defender for Office 365 include impersonation protection that detects when external senders use display names similar to specified VIP users (e.g., CEO, CFO). You configure: users to protect (specific high-value targets), domains to protect (your organization's domains), and actions when impersonation is detected (quarantine, junk, or deliver with tip). Mailbox intelligence enhances detection by learning each user's communication patterns.
Safe Links provides time-of-click URL scanning. It protects against malicious links but doesn't detect sender impersonation.
Anti-spam policies filter bulk email and spam based on content characteristics. They don't specifically detect display name impersonation or BEC attacks.
questions.tip: Anti-phishing impersonation protection: User impersonation → protect specific users (CEO, CFO, VIPs). Domain impersonation → protect specific domains (yours + partners). Mailbox intelligence → learns user communication patterns, flags anomalies. Actions: quarantine, junk email, deliver with safety tip. Tips shown to users: 'This sender appears similar to someone you've communicated with, but may not be that person.' Configure in: Defender portal → Policies → Anti-phishing. Requires: Defender for Office 365 Plan 1+.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization uses Intune to manage Windows devices
- A user reports they cannot access corporate resources after a recent Windows update
- The Intune portal shows the device as 'Not compliant'
- The non-compliance reason is: 'Require BitLocker' — BitLocker protection is suspended

Question:
What most likely happened and how should you resolve it?
choices: BitLocker was permanently disabled by the user — re-enable BitLocker manually
Windows Update automatically suspended BitLocker during the update — BitLocker will resume automatically after reboot, then compliance will re-evaluate
The BitLocker encryption key was lost — re-encrypt the entire drive
The compliance policy is incorrect — remove the BitLocker requirement
explanations: Users typically cannot permanently disable BitLocker without admin privileges. The scenario specifically mentions a recent Windows update, which is the most common cause of temporary BitLocker suspension.

This option is correct. Windows Update routinely suspends BitLocker protection temporarily during certain updates (especially firmware or UEFI updates). This is normal and expected behavior. BitLocker automatically resumes after the device reboots and the update completes. Once BitLocker resumes, the next Intune compliance check will evaluate the device as compliant again. The resolution is usually to simply wait for the update to complete and the device to reboot.
BitLocker keys are not lost during Windows updates. The recovery key remains stored in Azure AD. The suspension is temporary and keys are intact.
Removing the compliance requirement weakens security posture for all devices. The BitLocker requirement is correct — the temporary suspension during updates is expected and self-resolving.
questions.tip: BitLocker suspension during updates: Normal behavior for firmware/UEFI updates. Auto-resumes after reboot. Compliance evaluation: temporary non-compliance during suspension. Resolution: wait for update completion + reboot. If BitLocker doesn't resume: check device for issues, force resume via PowerShell (Resume-BitLocker). Compliance grace period: configure non-compliance actions with delay to avoid blocking during expected suspensions.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization uses Azure AD with Conditional Access
- The security team wants to ensure that users can only access Microsoft 365 from compliant corporate devices
- Personal devices should be completely blocked from accessing any Microsoft 365 service
- The policy must cover Exchange Online, SharePoint, Teams, and all other M365 apps

Question:
Which Conditional Access configuration blocks personal device access while allowing compliant corporate devices?
choices: Block all access from devices not marked as compliant by requiring device compliance for all cloud apps
Create a DLP policy that blocks data access from personal devices
Disable external access in Exchange Online admin centre
Remove Microsoft 365 licences from users who use personal devices
explanations: This option is correct. Create a Conditional Access policy: Users = All users (exclude break-glass). Cloud apps = All cloud apps (or Office 365 suite). Grant = Require device to be marked as compliant. This means only Intune-enrolled devices that pass compliance checks can access Microsoft 365. Personal devices not enrolled in Intune cannot be marked as compliant, so they're automatically blocked.
DLP policies control data sharing based on content, not device enrolment status. DLP cannot block device access based on whether the device is managed or personal.
Disabling external access in Exchange only affects Exchange Online and doesn't cover SharePoint, Teams, or other M365 services. It's also not based on device compliance state.
Removing licences prevents those users from accessing M365 entirely, not just from personal devices. This is punitive rather than protective and blocks access from corporate devices too.
questions.tip: Device compliance CA pattern: Require compliant device → only Intune-enrolled, policy-passing devices get access. Unmanaged devices → can't be compliant → blocked. Managed but non-compliant → also blocked until remediated. For BYOD: consider alternative patterns: app protection policy (MAM) or app-enforced restrictions for limited access. All-or-nothing corporate device only: require compliance. Balanced BYOD: require app protection for unmanaged, compliance for managed.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your company uses Microsoft Intune
- The IT team needs to understand which applications are installed across all managed Windows devices
- They want to see: application name, version, publisher, and how many devices have each app installed
- This information should be available without installing additional agents

Question:
Where can the IT team find this application inventory data?
choices: Azure AD admin centre → Enterprise applications
Intune admin centre → Apps → Discovered apps
Windows Event Viewer on each device
explanations: Azure AD Enterprise applications shows cloud/SaaS apps registered in Azure AD (OAuth apps, gallery apps). It doesn't show locally installed Windows applications on devices.

This option is correct. Intune's Discovered apps (Apps → Monitor → Discovered apps) shows an inventory of all applications detected on managed devices. For each app: name, version, publisher, and device install count. Intune collects this data automatically during device check-ins without requiring additional agents. You can filter and search the inventory to find specific applications across your entire managed fleet.
Microsoft 365 admin centre apps section manages M365 service-level app settings, not device-level application inventory.
Checking Event Viewer on each individual device doesn't scale and doesn't provide centralized reporting across the fleet.
questions.tip: Intune app inventory: Discovered apps → auto-collected inventory of installed apps. Data: app name, version, publisher, device count. No additional agent needed (collected by Intune MDM client). Filter by: platform (Windows, iOS, Android, macOS). Individual device: Devices → select device → Discovered apps (per-device view). Limitations: may not capture all Win32 apps on first sync, data refreshes at check-in intervals.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization is implementing passwordless authentication
- The IT team wants users to sign in to Windows devices and Microsoft 365 using:
  - Facial recognition or fingerprint (biometric)
  - A device-specific PIN as a backup
  - NO traditional passwords

Question:
Which technology provides this passwordless Windows sign-in experience?
explanations: Smart cards require physical card readers and PKI infrastructure. While they provide strong authentication, they're not biometric and are less convenient than the passwordless experience described.

This option is correct. Windows Hello for Business (WHfB) provides passwordless authentication using biometrics (facial recognition via Windows Hello camera, fingerprint via reader) and a device-bound PIN as backup. The PIN is NOT a password — it's cryptographically bound to the device's TPM and never leaves the device. WHfB provides SSO to both Windows device sign-in and Microsoft 365/Azure AD resources.
FIDO2 security keys provide passwordless authentication but require a physical USB or NFC key. They don't use the device's built-in biometric sensors (camera, fingerprint reader) for authentication.
SMS OTP is considered a weak MFA method and is not passwordless — it typically supplements a password rather than replacing it. It also requires phone network availability.
questions.tip: Passwordless methods compared: Windows Hello for Business → biometric + device-bound PIN, built into Windows. FIDO2 security keys → physical key (USB/NFC), portable across devices. Microsoft Authenticator passwordless → phone-based, push notification approval. Certificate-based auth → smart cards/certificates. WHfB advantages: built-in (no extra hardware), biometric convenience, SSO to Windows + cloud. WHfB requirements: TPM 2.0, biometric hardware (camera/fingerprint), Azure AD or hybrid Azure AD joined.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization uses Microsoft Purview DLP
- A DLP policy for SharePoint blocks sharing of documents containing Australian Business Numbers (ABN)
- Users report that the policy is triggering too many false positives on documents that mention 'ABN' as an abbreviation but don't contain actual business numbers

Question:
How should you reduce false positives while still detecting real ABNs?
choices: Increase the confidence level threshold and instance count in the DLP policy rule
Switch from DLP to a retention policy
Allow all users to override DLP policy matches
explanations: Disabling the policy removes all protection, which is the opposite of the goal. The policy needs tuning, not removal.

This option is correct. Increasing the confidence level threshold (e.g., from Low to High) requires more corroborating evidence before triggering (the number must pass validation checks and appear near supporting keywords like 'Australian Business Number', 'ABN:', 'tax'). Increasing the instance count (e.g., from 1 to 3+) requires multiple ABNs in a document before triggering. Both adjustments reduce false positives while maintaining detection of documents that genuinely contain multiple validated ABNs.
Retention policies manage content lifecycle and don't detect sensitive information types or prevent sharing. Switching to retention doesn't address the data protection requirement.
Allowing unrestricted overrides defeats the purpose of the DLP policy. While limited overrides with justification can be appropriate, blanket override permission removes enforcement.
questions.tip: DLP tuning for false positives: Confidence level: Low (pattern match) → Medium (+ keywords) → High (+ corroborative evidence). Higher confidence = fewer false positives. Instance count: increase minimum count to avoid single-mention triggers. Exclusion: exclude specific sites/groups from policy scope. Test mode: run in simulation first to measure false positive rate. Custom SIT: create custom sensitive information type with stricter patterns. Override with justification: allows users to override with a reason (logged for audit).

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization manages Windows, iOS, Android, and macOS devices with Intune
- The IT team needs to create different enrolment restrictions for different device types:
  - Corporate devices: all platforms allowed, no device limit
  - BYOD users: only iOS and Android, maximum 2 devices per user
  - Contractors: only iOS, maximum 1 device

Question:
Which Intune feature manages these enrolment restrictions?
choices: Device enrolment restrictions (device type and device limit)
Compliance policies with device count rules
explanations: Conditional Access controls access after enrolment. It doesn't restrict which device types can enrol or limit the number of enrolled devices per user.

This option is correct. Intune device enrolment restrictions include two types: Device type restrictions (which platforms/OS versions can enrol — Windows, iOS, Android, macOS) and Device limit restrictions (maximum number of devices per user). Create multiple restriction policies with different priorities and assign them to different groups: corporate users get all platforms + unlimited devices, BYOD users get iOS/Android + 2 device limit, contractors get iOS only + 1 device limit.
Compliance policies evaluate enrolled device health. They don't control which devices can enrol or set per-user device count limits.

Azure AD device settings include a maximum device limit for device registration, but they don't provide the granular platform-specific restrictions or group-based targeting that Intune enrolment restrictions offer.
questions.tip: Enrolment restrictions: Device type restriction → allowed platforms, block personal devices, minimum OS version. Device limit restriction → max devices per user (1-15). Priority: lower number = higher priority. Multiple policies: assign to different groups with different priorities. Default policy: applies to all users (lowest priority). Group assignment: target specific Azure AD groups for differentiated policies. Platform blocking: independently control each platform (Windows, iOS, Android, macOS).

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization has Microsoft 365 E5
- The security team discovers that attackers are using OAuth consent phishing
- Attackers trick users into granting a malicious app access to their mailbox and files
- Once the user consents, the app accesses corporate data without needing the user's password

Question:
Which security feature helps detect and remediate malicious OAuth app grants?
choices: Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps — App governance
explanations: Defender for Endpoint monitors endpoint devices. OAuth consent grants occur at the identity/cloud layer, not the endpoint level.

This option is correct. App governance in Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps monitors OAuth apps and their permissions in your Microsoft 365 environment. It detects: apps with excessive permissions, apps from unverified publishers, apps with suspicious behavior patterns, and sudden spikes in data access. When a malicious app is detected, admins can disable the app and revoke its permissions. Combined with Azure AD consent settings, this provides defense against OAuth consent phishing.
Transport rules process email in transit. They can't detect or revoke OAuth application grants.
Windows Defender Firewall controls network traffic on endpoints. It has no visibility into OAuth application consent grants.
questions.tip: OAuth consent phishing defense layers: Prevention: Azure AD consent settings → restrict user consent to verified publishers + low-risk permissions. Detection: Defender for Cloud Apps → App governance monitors app behavior and permissions. Remediation: disable malicious app + revoke permissions + revoke user sessions. Admin consent workflow: require admin approval for high-privilege permissions. User education: train users to recognize suspicious consent prompts.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization uses Intune to manage Windows devices
- The IT team needs to deploy the Microsoft 365 Apps suite (Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, Teams)
- The deployment should use the Monthly Enterprise Channel
- Updates should be managed by Intune, not by each device checking Office CDN directly

Question:
How should you configure the update delivery for Microsoft 365 Apps?
choices: Let each device download updates directly from the Office CDN (default behavior)
Configure Microsoft 365 Apps to use a local network share as the update source
Use the Intune Microsoft 365 Apps configuration profile to manage updates including delivery optimization
Disable all automatic updates and manually install updates
explanations: Direct CDN downloads work but consume internet bandwidth as each device downloads separately. For managed deployments, centralised update management provides more control.
A local network share requires maintaining an on-premises update repository and doesn't integrate with Intune's cloud management. This is the traditional SCCM approach, not the cloud-native approach.

This option is correct. The Intune Microsoft 365 Apps configuration profile manages the entire deployment including update channel (Monthly Enterprise), update management, and Delivery Optimization (peer-to-peer caching so devices share downloaded updates on the local network, reducing internet bandwidth). Intune provides visibility into update status and compliance across the fleet.
Disabling automatic updates leaves devices unpatched and vulnerable. Manual updates don't scale and provide no compliance reporting.
questions.tip: Microsoft 365 Apps update management in Intune: Configure via: Apps → Windows → Microsoft 365 Apps configuration. Update channel: Monthly Enterprise, Current, Semi-Annual Enterprise. Delivery Optimization: peer-to-peer sharing of update content (reduces bandwidth). Target version: pin to a specific build for testing. Deadline: force update installation by a date. Monitoring: Intune reports on M365 Apps update compliance. Cloud Update: Microsoft-managed update service for M365 Apps (newest option).

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization uses Azure AD and Intune
- The IT team needs to register IoT devices that don't support traditional Azure AD join
- These devices need limited access to specific cloud services
- The devices don't have a user associated with them

Question:
Which Azure AD registration type is appropriate for these IoT devices?
explanations: Azure AD join is designed for Windows devices that become fully managed by the organization. IoT devices with limited OS capabilities may not support the full Azure AD join process.
Hybrid Azure AD join requires on-premises Active Directory membership. IoT devices typically don't support domain joining.
Azure AD registered is for BYOD personal devices where users add their work account. IoT devices don't have users associated with them.

This option is correct. Azure IoT Hub provides device identity registration specifically designed for IoT devices. IoT Hub supports device provisioning at scale, device-to-cloud and cloud-to-device communication, and device twin management. For IoT devices that need to connect to Azure services, IoT Hub is the appropriate registration and management platform, not Azure AD.
questions.tip: Device identity types: Azure AD joined → corporate Windows devices, cloud-managed. Hybrid Azure AD joined → existing AD devices, cloud + on-premises. Azure AD registered → BYOD personal devices. Azure IoT Hub → IoT devices, sensors, edge devices. For managed endpoints (Windows, macOS, iOS, Android): Azure AD + Intune. For IoT/edge: Azure IoT Hub + IoT Edge. Don't confuse Azure AD device registration with IoT device registration — different platforms for different device types.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization has Microsoft 365 E5
- The security team is responding to a confirmed ransomware incident
- Several devices are actively encrypting files
- The team needs to take immediate action across all affected devices simultaneously

Question:
What is the recommended FIRST response action in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint?
choices: Run a full antivirus scan on all devices
Isolate all affected devices from the network immediately
Collect investigation packages from all affected devices
Create a new compliance policy requiring antivirus updates
explanations: A full antivirus scan takes time and doesn't prevent the ransomware from continuing to encrypt files and spreading to other devices during the scan.

This option is correct. During an active ransomware attack, the FIRST priority is containment — isolating affected devices from the network to prevent lateral movement and further encryption. Defender for Endpoint's network isolation cuts all network connections except the Defender cloud service connection, allowing continued remote investigation. After isolation, proceed with investigation and remediation.
Collecting investigation packages is important for forensics but doesn't stop the active attack. Containment must come before evidence collection.
Creating a new compliance policy is a long-term improvement, not an incident response action. It won't help during an active ransomware attack.
questions.tip: Ransomware incident response order: 1. ISOLATE affected devices (contain the spread). 2. Identify scope (which devices, which files, what variant). 3. Investigate (how did it get in, patient zero). 4. Remediate (remove malware, restore from backup). 5. Recover (bring devices back online). 6. Improve (close the entry point, strengthen defenses). Defender for Endpoint isolation: immediate, reversible, maintains Defender cloud connection. Multi-device isolation: can isolate multiple devices simultaneously from the Defender portal.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization is deploying 300 new Windows 11 laptops
- The devices will be Azure AD joined and managed by Intune
- Users need seamless single sign-on to Microsoft 365 and on-premises web applications
- On-premises web apps use Kerberos authentication

Question:
Which feature enables SSO to on-premises Kerberos-based applications from Azure AD joined devices?
choices: Azure AD Kerberos authentication (cloud Kerberos trust)
explanations: Azure AD Application Proxy publishes on-premises web apps externally without VPN, but the question asks about SSO using Kerberos from Azure AD joined devices, which is specifically handled by cloud Kerberos trust.

This option is correct. Azure AD Kerberos (cloud Kerberos trust) allows Azure AD joined devices to obtain Kerberos tickets for on-premises resources without needing line-of-sight to a domain controller. Azure AD acts as the Kerberos Key Distribution Centre for cloud-joined devices, enabling seamless SSO to on-premises Kerberos-authenticated web apps, file shares, and other resources.
A VPN provides network connectivity but doesn't solve the SSO/Kerberos authentication challenge. VPN + traditional Kerberos requires hybrid Azure AD join, not just a network path.

Hybrid Azure AD join would solve the Kerberos SSO problem but requires on-premises AD domain membership. The scenario specifies Azure AD joined (cloud-only) devices. Cloud Kerberos trust enables Kerberos SSO without on-premises domain membership.
questions.tip: SSO to on-premises from Azure AD joined devices: Cloud Kerberos trust → Kerberos tickets from Azure AD (no domain controller needed). Azure AD Application Proxy → publish on-premises apps externally (pre-authentication via Azure AD). Windows Hello for Business with cloud Kerberos trust → passwordless SSO to on-premises. Requirements: Azure AD Connect syncing, Azure AD Kerberos server object configured.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization has Microsoft 365 E5
- The security team wants to create custom detection rules using KQL (Kusto Query Language)
- The detections should query across email, endpoint, identity, and cloud app data
- When a detection triggers, it should automatically create an alert and optionally take response actions

Question:
Which Microsoft 365 Defender feature enables custom KQL-based threat detections?
choices: Alert policies in the Microsoft 365 compliance centre
Custom detection rules in Advanced hunting
explanations: Alert policies in the compliance centre create alerts based on predefined activity types (admin actions, user activities). They don't support custom KQL queries across Defender data tables.

This option is correct. Custom detection rules in Microsoft 365 Defender's Advanced hunting allow you to write KQL queries that run on a schedule (every 1, 3, 12, or 24 hours). When the query returns results, it creates alerts and optionally takes automated actions (isolate device, disable user, quarantine email). The queries can span all Defender data tables: email events, endpoint events, identity events, and cloud app events.

Microsoft Sentinel analytics rules also use KQL but operate in the Sentinel SIEM environment. The question asks about Microsoft 365 Defender specifically. Sentinel is a separate platform (though they can integrate).
Mail flow rules process email based on conditions but don't support KQL queries or cross-domain threat detection.
questions.tip: Custom detection rules: Write KQL in Advanced hunting → save as custom detection. Schedule: 1h, 3h, 12h, 24h. Actions: create alert, isolate device, disable user, quarantine email, run investigation. Data tables: DeviceProcessEvents, EmailEvents, IdentityLogonEvents, CloudAppEvents, etc. Use cases: detect specific attack patterns, hunt for IoCs, monitor suspicious activity. Best practice: test query in Advanced hunting first, then convert to custom detection.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization uses Intune to manage Windows devices
- The IT team needs to ensure that the Company Portal app is installed on all managed Windows devices
- Company Portal provides users with a self-service app catalog and device management actions
- The app should install automatically without user intervention

Question:
How should you deploy the Company Portal app to managed Windows devices?
choices: Tell users to download Company Portal from the Microsoft Store manually
Deploy Company Portal as a Required app from the Microsoft Store (new) or offline package via Intune
Company Portal is automatically installed during Intune enrolment on all platforms
Deploy Company Portal as a Win32 app by wrapping the installer
explanations: Manual download depends on user action and doesn't ensure Company Portal is on all devices. Users may not install it, leaving them without the self-service catalog.

This option is correct. Deploy Company Portal as a Required app in Intune. You can use the Microsoft Store app (new) type which pulls directly from the Microsoft Store, or deploy the offline-licensed Company Portal package. Assigning as Required ensures automatic installation on all targeted devices without user action. Company Portal is NOT automatically installed on Windows during Intune enrolment (unlike iOS/Android where it's part of the enrolment flow).
Company Portal is automatically installed on iOS and Android during enrolment, but NOT on Windows. On Windows, Company Portal must be explicitly deployed as an app through Intune.
Wrapping Company Portal as a Win32 app is unnecessary when the Microsoft Store (new) app type is available. The Store app type handles installation and updates automatically.
questions.tip: Company Portal deployment by platform: Windows → must be explicitly deployed (Microsoft Store app or offline package). iOS → installed during enrolment. Android → installed during enrolment (work profile or fully managed). macOS → must be explicitly deployed. Company Portal functions: self-service app catalog, device sync, compliance status, remote actions (rename, reset). Offline Company Portal: needed for Autopilot ESP and environments without Microsoft Store access.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization manages Windows devices with Intune
- The IT team receives reports that several devices show 'Not evaluated' for compliance status
- These devices have been enrolled in Intune for over a week
- The IT team has created compliance policies but the devices don't seem to be evaluating them

Question:
What is the most likely cause of 'Not evaluated' compliance status?
choices: The compliance policies are not assigned to the correct device or user groups
The devices don't have internet connectivity
The devices are running an unsupported Windows version
Intune service is experiencing an outage
explanations: This option is correct. 'Not evaluated' typically means no compliance policy is targeting the device. If compliance policies exist but aren't assigned to the group containing these devices, the devices have nothing to evaluate against. Check: is the compliance policy assigned to the correct Azure AD group? Is the device a member of that group? Also check: is the 'Mark devices with no compliance policy assigned as' setting configured to 'Not compliant' or 'Compliant'?
Devices without internet would show 'Pending' or stale data, not 'Not evaluated'. If they enrolled over a week ago, they had connectivity at some point.
Unsupported Windows versions would typically show the policy as 'Not applicable' rather than 'Not evaluated'. The compliance engine would still attempt evaluation.
A service outage would affect all devices, not just several. Other devices are presumably evaluating correctly.
questions.tip: Compliance status meanings: Compliant → passes all assigned policies. Not compliant → fails one or more policy checks. Not evaluated → no policy assigned to device. Pending → policy assigned but device hasn't checked in. In grace period → non-compliant but within grace period. Error → policy evaluation failed. Key setting: Compliance policies → Settings → 'Mark devices with no compliance policy as' → set to 'Not compliant' (recommended) to ensure unmanaged devices can't access resources.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization has Microsoft 365 E5
- The compliance team needs to respond to a GDPR Data Subject Access Request (DSAR)
- An employee requests a copy of all personal data the organization holds about them
- The data spans Exchange mailbox, OneDrive files, SharePoint sites, and Teams messages

Question:
Which Microsoft Purview tool helps fulfil this Data Subject Access Request?
choices: Data Subject Request (DSR) case in Microsoft Purview
explanations: DLP reports show policy matches for sensitive content. They don't collect all personal data about a specific person for a DSAR response.

This option is correct. Microsoft Purview provides a Data Subject Request (DSR) case workflow specifically for GDPR and privacy compliance. It uses Content search to find all data related to a specific person across Exchange, OneDrive, SharePoint, and Teams. The results can be reviewed, exported, and provided to the data subject. The DSR case manages the entire workflow: search, review, export, and close.
Retention policies manage content lifecycle but don't provide targeted search and export for a specific person's data.
Audit logs show user activities but don't search for all content containing a person's personal data across Microsoft 365 services.
questions.tip: Data Subject Request workflow: 1. Create DSR case in Microsoft Purview. 2. Search across all M365 locations for the data subject's information. 3. Review results for relevance. 4. Export data for the data subject. 5. Remediate (delete, rectify) if requested. 6. Close the case. GDPR rights covered: access, rectification, erasure, portability, restriction. DSR tools in Purview: Content search, eDiscovery, Azure AD (for identity data export).

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization has 500 Windows devices managed by Intune
- The security team requires that all devices have Secure Boot enabled
- Devices without Secure Boot should be marked as non-compliant
- Non-compliant devices must be blocked from accessing corporate resources

Question:
Which Intune feature checks for Secure Boot status on managed devices?
choices: Device configuration profile with UEFI settings
Device compliance policy with device health attestation (Secure Boot required)
explanations: Device configuration profiles push settings to devices but don't evaluate compliance state. Secure Boot is a firmware-level setting that can't be enabled through an Intune configuration profile — it must be enabled in the device BIOS/UEFI.

This option is correct. Device compliance policies in Intune include device health attestation checks, including Secure Boot. The Windows Health Attestation Service validates that Secure Boot is enabled on the device. If Secure Boot is not enabled, the compliance policy marks the device as non-compliant. Combined with Conditional Access requiring device compliance, non-compliant devices are blocked from corporate resources.
Endpoint security antivirus profiles manage Windows Defender Antivirus settings. They don't check Secure Boot firmware status.
Windows Update rings manage update delivery and restart settings. They have no relation to Secure Boot or firmware configuration.
questions.tip: Device health attestation checks in compliance policy: Secure Boot → verify Secure Boot enabled. BitLocker → verify drive encryption. Code integrity → verify code integrity checks enabled. Require TPM → verify TPM chip present. How it works: Windows Health Attestation Service (cloud-based) validates device boot integrity using TPM measurements. The compliance policy checks the attestation result. Requirements: TPM 2.0, UEFI firmware, Health Attestation Service connectivity.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your company uses Microsoft Intune
- The IT team deploys a line-of-business (LOB) iOS app (.ipa file) to managed devices
- The app was built with an enterprise distribution certificate
- After several months, users report the app crashes immediately on launch
- Investigation reveals the enterprise distribution certificate has expired

Question:
What must be done to resolve this issue?
choices: Ask users to reinstall the app from the App Store
Renew the enterprise distribution certificate, re-sign the app with the new certificate, and redeploy through Intune
