Reset the devices to factory settings
Change the app deployment from Required to Available
explanations: LOB apps are not available in the public App Store. They're internally distributed through Intune using enterprise certificates. The App Store has no record of the app.

This option is correct. When an enterprise distribution certificate expires, all apps signed with that certificate stop working (crash on launch). To fix: 1) Renew the certificate in the Apple Developer Enterprise portal. 2) Re-sign the .ipa with the new certificate. 3) Upload the re-signed .ipa to Intune. 4) Intune pushes the updated app to all devices. The app will work again once the re-signed version is installed.
Factory reset is extremely disruptive and doesn't address the root cause (expired certificate). The app would still fail after re-enrolment until the certificate is renewed.
Changing assignment type from Required to Available doesn't fix the expired certificate. The app would still crash regardless of how it's assigned.
questions.tip: iOS enterprise certificate management: Enterprise certificates expire every 3 years. Expired cert → all apps signed with it stop working. Remediation: renew cert → re-sign app → redeploy. Prevention: track certificate expiry dates, renew before expiration. Apple push notification certificate (APNs): expires annually — if this expires, ALL iOS management stops. Critical dates to track: APNs cert (annual), enterprise distribution cert (3 years), VPP token (annual).

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization has hybrid Azure AD joined Windows devices
- Azure AD Connect is synchronising device objects from on-premises AD to Azure AD
- The IT team notices that some devices appear as 'Pending' in Azure AD device registration
- These devices have been domain-joined for months but haven't completed hybrid Azure AD join

Question:
What is the most common cause of devices stuck in 'Pending' hybrid Azure AD join?
choices: The devices don't have internet connectivity to reach Azure AD endpoints
Azure AD Connect is not configured to sync device objects
The devices are running Windows 7 which is not supported
The Service Connection Point (SCP) is not configured in on-premises AD or the device can't reach Azure AD device registration endpoints
explanations: While internet connectivity is needed, devices stuck in 'Pending' for months typically have a configuration issue rather than a temporary connectivity problem.

If Azure AD Connect wasn't syncing device objects, the devices wouldn't appear in Azure AD at all — not even as 'Pending'. The fact that they show as 'Pending' means the device object has been synced but registration hasn't completed.
Windows 7 is no longer supported for hybrid Azure AD join in current configurations, but the scenario doesn't specify Windows 7. This is less common than SCP issues.

This option is correct. The most common cause of 'Pending' hybrid Azure AD join is: the Service Connection Point (SCP) is not configured in on-premises AD (the device can't discover the Azure AD tenant), OR the device can't reach Azure AD device registration endpoints (https://enterpriseregistration.windows.net). The SCP tells the device which Azure AD tenant to register with. Without it, the device can't complete the join process.
questions.tip: Hybrid Azure AD join troubleshooting: 1. Verify SCP: dsregcmd /status → check TenantName and TenantId. 2. Verify connectivity: device must reach enterpriseregistration.windows.net and login.microsoftonline.com. 3. Verify Azure AD Connect: device sync enabled in Connect options. 4. Check device: dsregcmd /status → AzureAdJoined should be YES. Common SCP issues: not configured, configured with wrong tenant, not accessible by device. Tools: dsregcmd /status (device-side), Azure AD Connect sync status (server-side).

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization has Microsoft 365 E5
- The security team wants to protect against credential theft on Windows devices
- Specifically, they want to prevent attackers from extracting password hashes from the LSASS process
- The solution should work on Azure AD joined devices managed by Intune

Question:
Which Windows security feature protects credentials in the LSASS process?
explanations: BitLocker encrypts the disk at rest, protecting data if the device is stolen while powered off. It doesn't protect the LSASS process from credential extraction while the system is running.

This option is correct. Windows Defender Credential Guard uses virtualisation-based security (VBS) to isolate the LSASS process in a protected container. Even if an attacker gains admin access to the device, they cannot extract password hashes, Kerberos tickets, or NTLM hashes from the isolated LSASS. This prevents pass-the-hash and pass-the-ticket attacks from the device. Configure via Intune device configuration profile.
Windows Firewall controls network traffic. It doesn't protect in-memory credentials from extraction by malware running locally.
Controlled folder access protects designated folders from unauthorized modification (anti-ransomware). It doesn't protect the LSASS credential process.
questions.tip: Credential Guard: Protects: NTLM hashes, Kerberos TGTs, credentials stored by applications. Uses: virtualisation-based security (VBS) + Hyper-V. Requirements: Windows 10/11 Enterprise, UEFI, Secure Boot, TPM (recommended), 64-bit CPU with virtualisation extensions. Configure via Intune: device configuration → Endpoint protection → Credential Guard. Cannot protect: local account passwords, credentials for services. Complementary: ASR rules can also protect LSASS (block credential stealing from lsass.exe).

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization uses Intune to manage Android devices
- Users need to access a corporate web application on their Android devices
- The web app should appear as an icon on the device home screen alongside other managed apps
- The web app URL is https://portal.company.com

Question:
How should you deploy this web app to managed Android Enterprise devices?
choices: Create a managed Google Play web app in the Managed Google Play iframe within Intune
Send users a link via email and ask them to bookmark it
Deploy a custom Android APK that opens the URL
Configure the URL in a device configuration profile
explanations: This option is correct. In Intune, you can create web apps through the Managed Google Play iframe. Navigate to Apps → Android → Add → Managed Google Play app → click the web app icon. Enter the URL, title, and icon. The web app is published to Managed Google Play and can be assigned like any other managed app. It appears as an icon on the device home screen and opens the URL in the default browser.
Email links provide no management, no home screen icon, and rely on users to take action. This is not an enterprise deployment approach.
Building a custom APK just to open a URL is unnecessary engineering when Managed Google Play natively supports web apps.
Device configuration profiles manage device settings, not app deployment. There's no web app URL setting in device configuration profiles.
questions.tip: Web apps on Android Enterprise: Create in Managed Google Play iframe → add title, URL, icon. Assign as Required (auto-install) or Available (user installs). The web app appears as a home screen icon. Opens in: default browser or managed browser (if configured). Alternative: web link app type in Intune (simpler but less integrated with Managed Google Play). iOS equivalent: web clip (same concept, different platform terminology).

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization wants to implement a Zero Trust security model
- The IT team needs to verify device health before granting access to resources
- Verification should check: OS version, antivirus status, encryption, and firewall status
- Devices failing any check should be denied access until remediated

Question:
Which Intune and Azure AD features implement this Zero Trust device verification?
choices: Azure AD B2B guest access policies
Intune compliance policies + Conditional Access requiring device compliance
Microsoft Defender for Endpoint threat score only
explanations: B2B guest access controls external user access. It doesn't verify device health for internal users' devices.

This option is correct. Zero Trust device verification: 1) Intune compliance policies check device health (OS version, antivirus active, BitLocker enabled, firewall on). 2) Devices passing all checks are marked 'Compliant'. 3) Conditional Access policy requires device compliance for resource access. 4) Non-compliant devices are blocked until remediated. This implements the Zero Trust principle: 'never trust, always verify' — every device access request is validated against health requirements.

Defender for Endpoint risk score provides threat-level assessment but is just one signal. The question asks about comprehensive device health verification (OS, AV, encryption, firewall), which requires compliance policies. Defender risk score can be included IN a compliance policy as one of many checks.
Password protection policies manage password content (banned words). They don't verify device health or implement Zero Trust device verification.
questions.tip: Zero Trust device pillars: 1. Compliance policy → verify device health (OS, encryption, antivirus, firewall, jailbreak). 2. Conditional Access → enforce access based on compliance. 3. Defender for Endpoint risk score → include threat level in compliance. 4. Continuous evaluation → re-check at each access and periodic sync. Zero Trust principle: assume breach, verify explicitly, least privilege access. Device trust is ONE pillar — also need identity verification, app protection, network controls.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization uses Microsoft Defender for Endpoint
- The security team wants to reduce the attack surface on managed Windows devices
- They want to block:
  - Office applications from creating child processes
  - JavaScript and VBScript from launching downloaded content
  - Credential stealing from the LSASS process

Question:
Which Defender for Endpoint feature blocks these specific attack techniques?
explanations: EDR detects and investigates threats after they occur. It doesn't proactively block specific attack techniques before they execute.

This option is correct. Attack surface reduction (ASR) rules block specific behaviors commonly used by malware: 'Block Office applications from creating child processes' prevents macro-based malware spawning PowerShell. 'Block JavaScript or VBScript from launching downloaded executable content' prevents script-based attacks. 'Block credential stealing from LSASS' prevents tools like Mimikatz from extracting credentials. Each rule can be set to: Block, Audit, Warn, or Disabled.
Automated investigation handles alerts by automatically investigating and remediating threats. It doesn't proactively block attack techniques.
Web content filtering blocks access to websites by category. It doesn't control application behavior on the endpoint.
questions.tip: Key ASR rules: Block Office from creating child processes. Block Office from creating executable content. Block JavaScript/VBScript launching downloaded content. Block credential stealing from LSASS. Block executable content from email. Block untrusted/unsigned processes from USB. Block persistence through WMI event subscription. Deployment: Audit mode first (monitor without blocking) → Block mode after testing. Configure via Intune: Endpoint security → Attack surface reduction.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization uses Intune with app protection policies
- The IT team configures an app protection policy for Microsoft Outlook on iOS
- The policy settings include:
  - Require PIN: Yes (6-digit)
  - Allow fingerprint: Yes
  - Offline grace period: 720 minutes (12 hours)
  - Minimum app version: 4.2

Question:
What happens if a user's Outlook app version is 4.1 (below the minimum)?
choices: Outlook works normally with no restrictions
The user receives a warning but can continue using Outlook
The user is blocked from accessing Outlook until they update to version 4.2 or later
The app protection policy is automatically disabled
explanations: Below-minimum app version triggers the conditional launch action. The app does NOT work normally.
By default, the minimum app version condition blocks access (not just warns). Warn is a separate configurable action.

This option is correct. When the app version is below the configured minimum, the conditional launch setting blocks the user from accessing the app. The user sees a message indicating they need to update the app. After updating to version 4.2 or later from the App Store, the app protection policy allows access. This ensures users are running a version with known security fixes.
The policy remains active. It's the policy that's enforcing the version check. The policy doesn't disable itself based on app version.
questions.tip: App protection policy conditional launch conditions: Min app version → block or warn if app is outdated. Min OS version → block or warn if OS is outdated. Max PIN attempts → wipe data after too many wrong PINs. Offline grace period → wipe or block after offline too long. Jailbroken/rooted device → block or wipe. Actions per condition: Block access, Warn (notify but allow), Wipe data. Best practice: set minimum app version to ensure security patches are applied.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your company has Windows devices that are Azure AD joined and Intune managed
- Users frequently work from home and need to access on-premises file shares
- The IT team doesn't want to set up a traditional VPN
- The file shares should be accessible from anywhere with internet connectivity

Question:
Which Microsoft solution provides access to on-premises file shares without VPN?
choices: Azure File Sync with Azure Files cloud tiering
Mapped network drives via Group Policy
explanations: This option is correct. Azure File Sync synchronises on-premises file server shares with Azure Files in the cloud. Users can access files via SMB from anywhere (using Azure AD authentication), while the on-premises file server maintains a complete copy. Cloud tiering keeps frequently accessed files local and tiers cold files to Azure. This provides VPN-free access to traditional file shares.
OneDrive Known Folder Move redirects user profile folders (Desktop, Documents, Pictures) to OneDrive. It doesn't provide access to shared departmental file servers.
SharePoint libraries are a different paradigm — they require migrating content from file shares to SharePoint. The scenario asks about accessing EXISTING on-premises file shares.
Mapped network drives via GPO require network connectivity to the file server (typically VPN from home). This is the traditional approach that the scenario wants to avoid.
questions.tip: File access without VPN options: Azure File Sync → sync on-prem file shares to Azure Files (SMB access anywhere). Azure AD Application Proxy → publish on-prem web-based file access. Microsoft Tunnel → mobile VPN for iOS/Android (but this IS a VPN). SharePoint migration → move file shares to SharePoint Online (requires migration effort). OneDrive → user personal files (not shared departmental data). Azure File Sync best for: existing file share infrastructure, gradual cloud migration, branch office scenarios.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization has Microsoft 365 E5
- The compliance team implements a DLP policy for Microsoft Teams
- The policy detects when users share credit card numbers in Teams chat messages
- When detected, the message should be blocked and the user should see a policy tip

Question:
What happens when a user sends a Teams message containing a credit card number?
choices: The message is sent normally and no action is taken
The message is blocked from being sent, and the sender sees a DLP policy tip explaining why
The message is sent but the credit card number is automatically redacted
The entire Teams conversation is deleted
explanations: With a DLP policy configured to block, the message is NOT sent normally. The DLP engine evaluates the message before delivery.

This option is correct. DLP for Teams intercepts messages in near real-time. When a message containing a credit card number is detected and the policy action is 'block', the message is prevented from being sent. The sender sees a DLP policy tip explaining that the message was blocked because it contains sensitive information. The sender can edit the message to remove the sensitive content and resend.
DLP in Teams blocks the message, not redacts content. Content redaction is not a standard DLP action for Teams messages.
DLP doesn't delete conversations. It blocks the specific message containing the sensitive content. All previous messages in the conversation are unaffected.
questions.tip: DLP in Teams: Applies to: chat messages and channel messages. Actions: block message, notify user (policy tip), notify admin, generate incident report. Policy tip: user sees inline notification explaining why message was blocked. User options: edit message and resend, override if allowed. Scope: internal messages, external/guest messages. Detection: sensitive info types, exact data match, trainable classifiers. Near real-time: messages evaluated as they're sent.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization has 200 macOS devices managed by Intune
- The IT team needs to deploy custom shell scripts to configure system preferences
- The scripts need to run with root privileges
- Script execution status must be monitored from the Intune portal

Question:
How should you deploy shell scripts to managed macOS devices through Intune?
choices: Email the scripts to users and ask them to run them in Terminal
Upload shell scripts in Intune under Devices → macOS → Shell scripts
Deploy scripts as macOS LOB apps
Use Apple Configurator to push scripts via USB
explanations: Email distribution provides no management, relies on user action, and users may not have root privileges to execute the scripts.

This option is correct. Intune provides a dedicated shell script deployment feature for macOS: Devices → macOS → Shell scripts. Upload the .sh file, configure: run as root or user, retry behavior, script frequency. The Intune management agent executes the script on targeted devices. Execution status (success/failure/pending) is reported in the Intune portal for monitoring.
Shell scripts are not applications and shouldn't be deployed as LOB apps. LOB apps have different lifecycle management (detection rules, install/uninstall) that doesn't apply to scripts.
Apple Configurator requires USB connection and doesn't support macOS devices for script deployment. It's for iOS/iPadOS device setup.
questions.tip: macOS shell scripts in Intune: Location: Devices → macOS → Shell scripts. Settings: run as signed-in user or root, hide script notifications, max retries, retry delay. Execution: Intune management agent (Microsoft Intune Agent) runs the script. Monitoring: per-device status in Intune portal. Limitations: script output is logged but not returned to portal. Best practice: include error handling and logging in scripts. The Intune agent must be installed (deployed separately for macOS).

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization has Microsoft 365 E5
- The security team wants to enable Continuous Access Evaluation (CAE)
- CAE should ensure that when a user account is disabled, access to Exchange Online and SharePoint Online is revoked within minutes (not hours)

Question:
What does Continuous Access Evaluation (CAE) do differently from standard token-based access?
choices: CAE eliminates the need for access tokens entirely
CAE enables resource providers to reject tokens in near real-time when critical events occur, rather than waiting for token expiry
CAE requires users to re-authenticate for every single request
CAE only works with on-premises applications
explanations: CAE still uses access tokens. It enhances the token lifecycle by enabling near real-time revocation, not by eliminating tokens.

This option is correct. Standard access tokens are valid for 60-90 minutes. If a user is disabled, their existing tokens continue working until expiry. CAE enables 'critical event evaluation' where resource providers (Exchange, SharePoint) subscribe to Azure AD events. When a critical event occurs (account disabled, password changed, high-risk detected, location changed), the resource provider rejects the existing token immediately, forcing re-authentication within minutes.
Requiring re-authentication for every request would destroy performance. CAE uses events-based evaluation — tokens are only challenged when specific events occur.
CAE works with Microsoft 365 cloud services (Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, Teams, Microsoft Graph). It's a cloud-native feature.
questions.tip: CAE critical events: User account disabled/deleted. Password changed. MFA enabled for user. Admin revokes refresh tokens. Azure AD Identity Protection detects high risk. CAE-aware clients: Outlook, Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint (web + desktop). CAE IP enforcement: if Conditional Access has location policies, CAE enforces IP changes in near real-time. Token lifetime with CAE: up to 28 hours (but revocable at any time). Without CAE: token valid until expiry (60-90 min).

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization uses Intune to manage Windows devices
- The IT team wants to deploy a set of fonts to all managed devices
- The fonts are needed for corporate branding in Office documents
- The fonts are packaged as .ttf files

Question:
What is the best way to deploy custom fonts to Intune-managed Windows devices?
choices: Email the font files to users and ask them to install manually
Package the fonts as a Win32 app (.intunewin) with a PowerShell install script that copies fonts to C:\Windows\Fonts and updates the registry
Deploy fonts through a device configuration profile
Upload fonts to SharePoint and tell users to download them
explanations: Manual installation via email is unreliable and doesn't scale. Users may not know how to install fonts properly.

This option is correct. Package the font files along with a PowerShell installation script into an .intunewin file using the Win32 Content Prep Tool. The script copies .ttf files to C:\Windows\Fonts and registers them in the registry (HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Fonts). Include a detection rule (check for font file in Fonts folder). Deploy as a Required Win32 app. This provides automated, managed font deployment.
Device configuration profiles don't have a font deployment option. Fonts are files that need to be copied and registered, which is an app/script deployment task.
SharePoint download requires user action and doesn't provide centralized management or installation verification.
questions.tip: Custom font deployment via Intune: 1. Create PowerShell script: copy .ttf to C:\Windows\Fonts, add registry entries. 2. Package with Win32 Content Prep Tool → .intunewin. 3. Upload to Intune as Win32 app. 4. Install command: PowerShell.exe -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File install_fonts.ps1. 5. Detection rule: file exists in C:\Windows\Fonts\fontname.ttf. 6. Assign as Required. Alternative: Intune PowerShell script deployment (simpler but less management features).

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your company has Windows devices enrolled in Intune
- The IT team needs to configure the Windows lock screen with:
  - Company logo displayed on the lock screen
  - A custom lock screen background image
  - Status information showing calendar and email
  - Lock screen timeout of 5 minutes

Question:
Which Intune profile type configures these lock screen settings?
choices: Device restriction profile (or Settings Catalog) with lock screen settings
explanations: Compliance policies evaluate device state. They don't configure lock screen appearance or behavior.

This option is correct. Device restriction profiles (or the Settings Catalog) allow configuring lock screen settings: lock screen image (custom background), company branding, status apps (calendar, email), and lock screen timeout. These settings are pushed to devices and enforce the corporate lock screen experience across all managed Windows devices.
App protection policies manage data protection within mobile apps. They don't configure Windows lock screen settings.
Windows Update rings manage update delivery and restart behavior. They have no lock screen configuration capabilities.
questions.tip: Lock screen configuration in Intune: Device restrictions → General → Lock screen: background image URL, timeout. Personalisation: Settings Catalog → search 'lock screen' or 'personalisation'. Company branding: Azure AD → Company branding (sign-in page + lock screen logo). Lock screen apps: configure status apps (calendar, email, notifications). Kiosk vs lock screen: kiosk replaces the shell, lock screen configures the idle/locked state. Image: must be hosted at an accessible URL (Azure Blob Storage works well).

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization has Microsoft 365 E5
- A departing employee's manager suspects they may have copied confidential files before leaving
- The security team needs to investigate:
  - Files downloaded from SharePoint in the last 30 days
  - USB file transfers detected by Defender for Endpoint
  - Emails sent to personal accounts
  - Print activities

Question:
Which Microsoft Purview solution correlates these activity signals for departing employee investigation?
choices: Insider Risk Management with 'Data theft by departing users' policy
explanations: Content search finds content by keywords/location but doesn't correlate user behavioral signals like download volumes, USB transfers, and print activities.

This option is correct. Insider Risk Management with the 'Data theft by departing users' policy template correlates multiple signals: SharePoint/OneDrive downloads, USB file transfers (from Defender for Endpoint), emails to personal accounts, printing activity, cloud storage uploads, and more. When integrated with an HR connector (providing departure/termination dates), it triggers enhanced monitoring 90 days before the departure date. Alerts show a risk timeline with all suspicious activities.
DLP reports show policy matches (sensitive content detected) but don't provide the holistic behavioral analysis of a departing employee's activities across multiple channels.
Communication compliance monitors message content for policy violations. It doesn't track file downloads, USB transfers, or print activities.
questions.tip: Insider Risk Management — departing employee scenario: HR connector: provides resignation/termination dates → triggers enhanced monitoring. Signals correlated: file downloads, USB transfers, email to personal addresses, cloud uploads, print volume, sequence detection. Timeline: 90 days before departure → departure date → 30 days after. Risk indicators: unusual download volume, first-time USB use, emailing to personal domains. Actions: generate alert → investigate case → escalate to eDiscovery if needed.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization has Intune-managed Windows devices
- The IT team needs to run a complex remediation script that:
  - Detects if the Windows Time service is configured correctly
  - If not, reconfigures the NTP server and restarts the service
  - Reports success or failure back to Intune
- The script should run every 6 hours

Question:
Which Intune feature is designed for this detect-and-fix pattern?
explanations: Device configuration profiles push settings but don't run custom scripts with detect/fix logic and scheduled execution.

This option is correct. Proactive remediations provide exactly this pattern: a detection script runs on schedule (configurable, including every 6 hours) to check a condition. If the detection script returns exit code 1 (issue found), the remediation script automatically runs to fix the issue. Both scripts report results back to Intune. The IT team can see: how many devices have the issue, how many were successfully remediated, and failure details.
Compliance policy custom scripts evaluate device state for compliance but don't remediate issues. They report compliance status, not fix problems.
Win32 apps are for application deployment, not for scheduled detect-and-fix operations. The lifecycle management (install/uninstall/detect) doesn't match the recurring remediation pattern.
questions.tip: Proactive remediations structure: Detection script: check condition → exit 0 (OK) or exit 1 (needs fix). Remediation script: fix the issue → exit 0 (success) or exit 1 (failed). Schedule: once, every 1h, 3h, 6h, 12h, 24h. Reporting: Intune shows detection rate, remediation rate, error rate. Script context: run as user or system (root). Use cases: fix misconfigured services, clear temp files, update registry, ensure required software is running. Requirements: Windows 10/11 Enterprise/Education, Intune licence.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization uses Azure AD with multiple Conditional Access policies
- Policy 1: Require MFA for all users to all cloud apps
- Policy 2: Block access from outside allowed countries
- Policy 3: Require compliant device for Exchange Online
- A user signs in from an allowed country on a non-compliant device to Exchange Online

Question:
What is the result of these three policies for this sign-in?
choices: Access is granted because the user is in an allowed country
Access is granted after completing MFA
Access is blocked because the device is not compliant (Policy 3), even though MFA is completed and location is allowed
Only Policy 1 applies because it was created first
explanations: Being in an allowed country satisfies Policy 2 but doesn't satisfy Policy 3 (device compliance). All applicable policies must be satisfied.
Completing MFA satisfies Policy 1 but doesn't satisfy Policy 3 (device compliance). The user needs to meet ALL applicable policy requirements.

This option is correct. Conditional Access policies are additive — ALL applicable policies must be satisfied for access to be granted. Policy 1 requires MFA (user must complete MFA). Policy 2 allows the country (satisfied). Policy 3 requires a compliant device for Exchange Online (NOT satisfied — device is non-compliant). Since Policy 3's requirement is not met, access is BLOCKED even though Policies 1 and 2 are satisfied. The most restrictive outcome applies.
Conditional Access policies don't have priority based on creation order. All applicable policies are evaluated simultaneously, and ALL must be satisfied.
questions.tip: Conditional Access evaluation: ALL applicable policies are evaluated. ALL grant controls from ALL matching policies must be satisfied. If ANY policy blocks → access blocked. Policies are additive (AND logic across policies). Within a single policy: grant controls can be AND or OR. Example: Policy A requires MFA AND Policy B requires compliance → user must satisfy BOTH. Exception: Block policy always wins over Grant policy. Best practice: use report-only mode to test policy combinations before enforcement.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your company manages Windows devices with Intune
- The IT team deploys Microsoft 365 Apps through Intune
- Users report that macro-enabled Excel files from trusted business partners are being blocked
- The macros are legitimate and required for business operations
- The IT team needs to allow macros from specific trusted locations while keeping macros blocked from untrusted sources

Question:
How should you configure macro settings through Intune?
choices: Disable all macro security to allow all macros
Configure Office cloud policy or Intune ADMX templates to define trusted locations and set macro security to 'Disable all except digitally signed macros'
Ask users to click 'Enable Content' on every macro-enabled file
Uninstall Microsoft 365 Apps and use web-only Office
explanations: Disabling all macro security allows ALL macros including malicious ones. This is a critical security risk and violates best practices.

This option is correct. Use Intune ADMX administrative templates or Office cloud policy to configure: Trusted locations (specific network paths or folders where macros are allowed), VBA macro notification settings ('Disable all except digitally signed macros' or 'Disable all with notification'), and macro security level. This allows legitimate macros from trusted partner files while blocking macros from untrusted/unknown sources.

Clicking 'Enable Content' on every file trains users to automatically click through security prompts, which is dangerous. It also doesn't provide centralized management or consistent policy enforcement.
Removing desktop Office eliminates macro support entirely, which breaks the business requirement for macro-enabled files.
questions.tip: Office macro security via Intune: ADMX templates: Microsoft Office → Security Settings → Trust Centre → Macro Settings. Trusted locations: define specific folders/paths where macros are allowed. Macro settings: Disable all without notification, Disable all with notification, Disable all except digitally signed, Enable all (NOT recommended). Best practice: trusted locations + digitally signed macros. Also consider: ASR rule 'Block Office apps from creating child processes' for additional protection against malicious macros.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization manages devices with Intune
- The IT team wants to implement a device naming convention for Windows Autopilot devices
- All devices should be named with the format: CORP-%SERIAL%
- The name should be applied automatically during Autopilot provisioning

Question:
Where do you configure the device name template for Autopilot?
choices: Windows Autopilot deployment profile → device name template
explanations: Azure AD device settings include a maximum device limit and default settings, but they don't provide device naming templates for Autopilot.

This option is correct. The Windows Autopilot deployment profile includes a device name template setting. You define a template using variables like %SERIAL% (device serial number) and %RAND:x% (random digits). For example: 'CORP-%SERIAL%' names the device 'CORP-ABC123XYZ'. The name is applied during the Autopilot OOBE process, and the device is renamed and restarted to apply the new name.
Compliance policies evaluate device state. They don't set device names.
Update rings manage Windows update behavior. They have no device naming capability.
questions.tip: Autopilot device name template: Variables: %SERIAL% (serial number), %RAND:x% (x random digits). Character limit: 15 characters total (NetBIOS limit). Examples: CORP-%SERIAL%, LAP-%RAND:6%, NYC-%SERIAL%. Restrictions: letters, numbers, hyphens only. No spaces or special characters. The template is set per Autopilot deployment profile, so different profiles can have different naming conventions. Device is renamed and restarted during Autopilot provisioning.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization uses Microsoft Purview
- The compliance team needs to implement a retention policy for SharePoint Online
- Requirements:
  - All documents in the Finance site must be retained for 10 years
  - After 10 years, documents should be reviewed by the records manager before deletion
  - Documents in all other sites should be retained for 3 years then automatically deleted

Question:
How should you configure retention to include a review before deletion?
choices: Create a retention policy with automatic deletion after 10 years
Create a retention label with 10-year retention and disposition review, auto-apply to the Finance site
Create an eDiscovery hold for 10 years
Configure SharePoint versioning to keep 10 years of versions
explanations: Automatic deletion after 10 years doesn't include a review step. The requirement explicitly states a records manager must review before deletion.

This option is correct. Retention labels support disposition review — when the retention period expires, instead of automatic deletion, reviewers are notified to review the content and approve or extend retention. Create a retention label with: 10-year retention, trigger disposition review at end of retention, assign reviewers (records manager). Auto-apply the label to the Finance site. A separate org-wide retention policy handles the 3-year auto-delete for other sites.
eDiscovery holds preserve content indefinitely until removed. They don't provide lifecycle management with timed retention and disposition review.
SharePoint versioning manages document versions but doesn't enforce retention periods or disposition review workflows.
questions.tip: Disposition review: Only available with retention labels (not retention policies). At end of retention: auto-delete OR trigger disposition review. Reviewers: specified users/groups receive notification to review items. Review actions: approve disposal (delete), extend retention, relabel, add reviewers. Disposition review is required for: regulatory records, high-value content, legal hold material. Records management: disposition review provides audit trail for compliance. Multi-stage disposition: items can go through multiple review stages.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization manages Windows devices with Intune
- The IT team wants to enable network-level protection on all managed devices
- The protection should block connections to known malicious domains and IP addresses
- It should work regardless of which browser or application makes the connection

Question:
Which Microsoft Defender for Endpoint feature provides this network-level protection?
explanations: Web content filtering blocks access to websites by category (adult, gambling, etc.) through the browser. It's browser-level filtering, not network-level protection against malicious domains.

This option is correct. Network protection extends Microsoft Defender SmartScreen protection to all network traffic on the device, not just browser traffic. It blocks outbound connections to known malicious domains, IP addresses, and URLs regardless of which application initiates the connection. This protects against malware callbacks, command-and-control communications, and phishing from any application.
Controlled folder access protects designated folders from unauthorized changes by untrusted applications. It's anti-ransomware, not network protection.
Exploit protection mitigates exploitation techniques (DEP, ASLR, CFG) at the application level. It doesn't filter network connections.
questions.tip: Network protection: Blocks outbound connections to malicious domains/IPs. Works at OS level → all applications (not just browsers). Uses SmartScreen reputation data. Modes: Block, Audit, Disabled. Configure via Intune: endpoint security → attack surface reduction or device configuration. Requires: Defender for Endpoint. Complements web content filtering: network protection = malicious sites, web filtering = category-based blocking.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization has Microsoft 365 E5
- The security team needs to investigate a phishing email that was delivered to 50 users
- They need to:
  - Find all instances of the email across all mailboxes
  - Remove the email from all affected mailboxes
  - Determine how many users clicked the link in the email

Question:
Which tool in Microsoft Defender for Office 365 enables this email investigation and remediation?
choices: Message trace in Exchange admin centre
explanations: Message trace tracks email delivery but doesn't show whether users clicked links or allow bulk removal of emails from mailboxes.

This option is correct. Threat Explorer in Defender for Office 365 Plan 2 (Real-time detections in Plan 1) allows security teams to: search for specific emails across all mailboxes (by sender, subject, URL, file hash), view delivery actions and locations, see URL click data (who clicked the malicious link), and take remediation actions like soft delete or hard delete the email from all affected mailboxes. This is the primary email threat investigation tool.
Quarantine management handles emails that were quarantined by email protection policies. It doesn't find emails that were delivered to inboxes or provide click analytics.
Anti-spam policy settings configure spam filtering rules. They don't provide investigation or remediation capabilities for specific email incidents.
questions.tip: Threat Explorer capabilities: Search: by sender, recipient, subject, URL, attachment hash, delivery action. Views: All email, Malware, Phish, Content malware. URL clicks: see who clicked, when, from which device. Remediation: soft delete, hard delete, move to junk, move to inbox (false positive). Requires: Defender for Office 365 Plan 2 (Threat Explorer) or Plan 1 (Real-time detections — limited). Email timeline: see the complete journey of an email through protection stack.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization uses Intune
- The IT team needs to deploy a Python-based internal tool to Windows devices
- The tool requires Python 3.11 runtime to be installed first
- Both Python 3.11 and the internal tool are packaged as Win32 apps in Intune

Question:
What should you configure to ensure Python installs before the internal tool?
choices: Assign both apps as Required and assume correct installation order
Configure Python 3.11 as a dependency of the internal tool app in Intune
Create a compliance policy requiring Python before deploying the tool
Deploy both apps in separate Intune tenants
explanations: Intune doesn't guarantee installation order for independently assigned apps. The internal tool might install before Python, causing it to fail.

This option is correct. Win32 app dependencies ensure prerequisite apps install first. Configure the internal tool app's dependency to include Python 3.11 with 'auto install' enabled. Intune will: 1) Check if Python 3.11 is detected, 2) If not, install Python first, 3) Wait for Python detection to succeed, 4) Then install the internal tool. This guarantees correct installation order.
Compliance policies evaluate device state but don't control app installation order or prerequisites.
You can't deploy apps across separate Intune tenants for the same devices. This is architecturally incorrect.
questions.tip: Win32 app dependency best practices: Auto install: set to Yes for dependencies that should be silently installed. Detection: dependency must have valid detection rules (Intune checks before proceeding). Chain: A depends on B depends on C → Intune installs C, B, A in order. Failure handling: if dependency fails to install, primary app installation is blocked. Circular dependencies: not allowed. Maximum depth: Intune limits dependency chain depth.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your company has iOS devices enrolled in Intune via Apple Business Manager
- The devices are supervised
- The IT team wants to remotely lock a lost supervised device and display a custom message on the lock screen
- The message should include a phone number to call if found

Question:
Which Intune remote action displays a custom message on a locked iOS device?
choices: Remote Lock (basic lock with no message)
Lost Mode (display custom message, phone number, and location tracking)
explanations: Remote Lock locks the device with the existing passcode but doesn't display a custom message or phone number on the lock screen.

This option is correct. Lost Mode (available for supervised iOS devices only) locks the device and displays a custom message and phone number on the lock screen. It also enables location tracking so IT can see where the device is. The device cannot be unlocked by the user until Lost Mode is disabled by the IT admin. This is ideal for lost or stolen corporate devices.
Wiping the device removes all data. This is a last resort for lost devices and doesn't help recover the device.
Disable Activation Lock removes the iCloud account association, allowing the device to be set up with a new account. It doesn't lock the device or display messages.
questions.tip: Lost Mode (iOS supervised only): Custom lock screen message + phone number. Location tracking (shows device on map). Device locked until IT disables Lost Mode. Sound: can play a sound to locate the device. Requirements: supervised device (ABM/ADE enrolled). Comparison: Remote Lock → basic lock, no message, works on all iOS. Lost Mode → message + tracking, supervised only. Wipe → last resort, removes all data. Best practice: try Lost Mode first, wipe only if recovery is impossible.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization has Microsoft 365 E5
- The compliance team needs to apply different DLP policies to different departments
- The Finance department should have strict DLP blocking for credit card and bank account numbers
- The Marketing department should have DLP monitoring only (no blocking) for the same sensitive data types
- All other departments should have no DLP policy

Question:
How should you scope these DLP policies?
choices: Create one DLP policy for the entire organization and hope it works for everyone
Create two separate DLP policies: one scoped to Finance group (block action) and one scoped to Marketing group (audit/monitor action)
Create DLP policies based on device type, not department
Configure DLP in the Exchange admin centre per mailbox
explanations: A single org-wide policy can't have different actions for different departments. It would apply the same action to everyone.

This option is correct. Create two DLP policies with different scopes and actions: Policy 1 targets the Finance group, detects credit card/bank account numbers, action = block. Policy 2 targets the Marketing group, detects the same data types, action = audit only (monitor and log without blocking). No policy targets other departments, so they're unaffected. Each policy is scoped to specific Azure AD groups or individual users.
DLP policy scoping by device type doesn't address the department-based requirement. The same device might be used by different departments.
Exchange admin centre DLP is the legacy approach. Modern DLP is managed in Microsoft Purview and can be scoped to users/groups across all M365 services, not just Exchange.
questions.tip: DLP policy scoping: Users/groups: include or exclude specific Azure AD groups. Locations: Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams, Endpoints, Power BI. Policy modes: Test without notifications (silent audit), Test with notifications (audit + tips), Turn on (enforce). Per-department approach: create separate policies per group with appropriate actions. Priority: when multiple policies match, all actions are applied. Location scoping: can target specific SharePoint sites within a policy.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization manages Android devices with Intune
- The IT team needs to configure email access on managed Android Enterprise work profile devices
- The email app should be Microsoft Outlook
- The email account should be automatically configured with the user's Exchange Online mailbox

Question:
How should you configure automatic email setup for Outlook on Android?
choices: Ask users to manually configure their email in Outlook
Deploy Outlook as a Required app and use an app configuration policy to pre-configure the Exchange Online account
Create a device configuration email profile for Android
Deploy the Gmail app with Exchange ActiveSync settings
explanations: Manual configuration relies on users knowing their email settings and doesn't ensure consistent configuration. It's not an enterprise management approach.

This option is correct. Deploy Microsoft Outlook as a Required app from Managed Google Play. Then create an app configuration policy that pre-configures the Exchange Online account using variables ({{mail}}, {{userPrincipalName}}). When the user opens Outlook for the first time, their mailbox is automatically configured without manual setup. This provides a seamless, consistent email experience.
Native Android email profiles in Intune configure the built-in email client, not Outlook. For Outlook-specific configuration, use an app configuration policy targeting Outlook.
Gmail is a personal email app and doesn't provide the managed email experience or integration with Intune app protection policies that Outlook provides.
questions.tip: Outlook auto-configuration on Android: 1. Deploy Outlook (Required, Managed Google Play). 2. App configuration policy → managed devices. 3. Configuration keys: com.microsoft.outlook.EmailProfile.EmailAccountName = {{username}}, com.microsoft.outlook.EmailProfile.EmailAddress = {{mail}}. 4. Combined with app protection policy for data protection. Auto-configuration variables: {{mail}}, {{userPrincipalName}}, {{username}}, {{displayName}}. Same approach works for iOS Outlook deployment.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization has Microsoft 365 E5
- The compliance team wants to understand what types of sensitive data exist across the organization
- They need a dashboard showing:
  - How many documents contain credit card numbers, SSNs, and other sensitive data
  - Where the sensitive data is located (Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive)
  - Which sensitivity labels have been applied across the organization

Question:
Which Microsoft Purview feature provides this data classification overview?
choices: Data classification → Overview and Content explorer
explanations: DLP reports show what DLP policies detected and what actions were taken. They don't provide a comprehensive classification overview of all data across the organization.

This option is correct. Data classification in Microsoft Purview provides: Overview dashboard showing counts of sensitive information types detected, sensitivity labels applied, and retention labels applied across the organization. Content explorer allows drilling into specific items to see what was detected and where. Activity explorer shows user activities related to labeled content. This gives the compliance team a complete picture of the organization's data landscape.
Audit log search shows user activities but doesn't classify or count sensitive data types across the organization.
eDiscovery content search finds specific content matching criteria but doesn't provide the aggregate classification overview and statistics.
questions.tip: Data classification in Microsoft Purview: Overview → aggregate counts of sensitive info types and labels. Content explorer → browse actual content items by classification. Activity explorer → user activities on classified content (label applied, label changed, file shared). Sensitive info types dashboard: top types detected, location distribution. Label dashboard: sensitivity labels applied by type, auto vs manual. Content explorer permissions: requires Content Explorer Content Viewer role.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization uses Intune to manage Windows devices
- Users need access to legacy web applications that only work in Internet Explorer mode
- The IT team wants to use Microsoft Edge as the default browser
- Specific intranet URLs should automatically open in IE mode within Edge

Question:
How should you configure IE mode in Microsoft Edge through Intune?
choices: Install Internet Explorer alongside Microsoft Edge
Configure an Edge site list (Enterprise Mode Site List XML) through Intune administrative templates or Settings Catalog
Use a completely separate browser for legacy sites
Rewrite all legacy web applications to work with modern browsers
explanations: Internet Explorer is deprecated and removed from Windows 11. IE mode in Edge provides backward compatibility without a separate browser installation.

This option is correct. Configure IE mode by creating an Enterprise Mode Site List (XML file) that specifies which URLs should open in IE mode. Deploy via Intune using Administrative Templates or Settings Catalog: 'Configure the Enterprise Mode Site List' → specify the URL to the hosted XML file. When users navigate to listed URLs in Edge, they automatically render in IE mode. All other sites render normally in Edge's Chromium engine.
Using a separate browser creates a fragmented user experience and doubles browser management. IE mode in Edge provides a unified browser experience.
Rewriting legacy applications is ideal long-term but requires significant development effort and budget. IE mode provides an immediate solution while applications are modernised.
questions.tip: IE mode in Edge: Enterprise Mode Site List: XML file listing URLs that need IE rendering. Host the XML: Azure Blob Storage, IIS server, or SharePoint. Configure via Intune: ADMX template → Microsoft Edge → 'Configure the Enterprise Mode Site List'. Site list XML format: <site url="intranet.company.com"><open-in>IE11</open-in></site>. Edge behavior: IE mode tabs show IE icon, render with IE engine. IE mode support: Microsoft committed to supporting until at least 2029. Cloud site list: can use Microsoft 365 admin centre to manage site list without XML.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization has Intune-managed Windows devices
- A new compliance requirement states that devices must have the latest Defender antivirus definitions (no older than 3 days)
- Devices with outdated definitions should be blocked from accessing corporate resources

Question:
How should you enforce this antivirus definition currency requirement?
choices: Create a PowerShell script that checks definition age daily
Create a compliance policy with 'Require antivirus definitions to be up to date' setting, integrated with Conditional Access
Create a device configuration profile that updates definitions
Send email reminders to users to update their antivirus
explanations: A PowerShell script can check definitions but doesn't integrate with Conditional Access for access blocking. It also doesn't provide the compliance reporting needed.

This option is correct. Intune compliance policies include Microsoft Defender Antivirus settings. Configure 'Require security intelligence to be up to date' which checks the age of antivirus definitions. Devices with definitions older than the threshold (configurable, including 3 days) are marked non-compliant. Combined with Conditional Access requiring device compliance, non-compliant devices are blocked from corporate resources until definitions are updated.

Device configuration profiles can configure Defender update schedules but don't evaluate compliance or block access based on definition currency. Configuration pushes settings; compliance checks state.
Email reminders provide no enforcement. Users may ignore them, and there's no access control mechanism.
questions.tip: Defender compliance settings: Require antivirus → Defender must be on. Require real-time protection → real-time scanning active. Require security intelligence to be up to date → definition age check. Require anti-spyware → anti-spyware enabled. Combined with Conditional Access: non-compliant devices are blocked. Defender updates: definitions update automatically (multiple times daily). If updates fail: check Windows Update, Defender service status, network connectivity.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization has Azure AD Premium P2
- The security team wants to review all users who have permanent Global Administrator role assignments
- They want to convert permanent assignments to eligible assignments that require activation
- A quarterly review process should verify that all privileged role assignments are still necessary

Question:
Which Azure AD feature provides these privileged role management capabilities?
choices: Azure AD Roles and administrators (standard role management)
explanations: Standard role management shows permanent assignments but doesn't provide eligible/active distinction, activation workflows, or access reviews.

This option is correct. Azure AD PIM provides: conversion of permanent role assignments to eligible (just-in-time) assignments, activation workflow with MFA/justification/approval requirements, time-limited role activation (e.g., 4-hour sessions), and access reviews (quarterly reviews where reviewers verify if users still need their role). PIM ensures privileged access follows least-privilege and just-in-time principles.
Conditional Access controls access to apps based on conditions. It doesn't manage Azure AD role assignments or provide access reviews for privileged roles.
Identity Protection detects risky sign-ins and compromised credentials. It doesn't manage role assignments or conduct access reviews.
questions.tip: PIM capabilities: Eligible vs Active: eligible = can activate when needed, active = always on. Activation: require MFA, justification, approval, time limit. Access reviews: periodic review of role assignments (who still needs this role?). Alerts: notify when roles are activated or permanently assigned. History: audit log of all activations and role changes. Best practice: no permanent Global Admin (except break-glass), all other admins = eligible via PIM. Access review outcomes: approve (keep), deny (remove), don't respond (configurable action).

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization has Windows devices enrolled in Intune
- The IT team needs to configure DNS settings on all managed devices
- Devices should use specific internal DNS servers (10.0.0.1, 10.0.0.2) when on the corporate network
- When off-network, devices should use standard public DNS

Question:
How should you handle network-aware DNS configuration for Intune-managed devices?
choices: Deploy a VPN profile with split DNS configuration that applies DNS settings based on network connection
Set static DNS on every device manually
Configure DNS in a compliance policy
Deploy a device configuration profile with static DNS settings that apply universally
explanations: This option is correct. A VPN profile with split DNS (or a VPN with DNS suffix rules) can configure devices to use specific DNS servers when connected to the corporate network (via VPN or direct connection) while using standard DNS when off-network. Alternatively, an always-on VPN with split tunnelling can route DNS queries for internal domains to corporate DNS servers while using public DNS for everything else.
Manual static DNS doesn't scale and causes issues when devices leave the corporate network — static corporate DNS servers won't resolve from external networks.
Compliance policies evaluate device state. They don't configure DNS settings.
Static DNS settings applied universally would break name resolution when the device is off the corporate network, as the internal DNS servers (10.0.0.x) wouldn't be reachable.
questions.tip: DNS configuration approaches: VPN with split DNS → corporate DNS for internal domains, public DNS for external. NRPT (Name Resolution Policy Table) → route specific domain queries to specific DNS servers. Wi-Fi profile → DNS settings per Wi-Fi network. Always-on VPN → persistent DNS configuration when VPN is connected. For Intune: VPN profile or Settings Catalog with NRPT rules provide network-aware DNS. Avoid static device-wide DNS as it breaks off-network resolution.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization has Microsoft 365 E5
- An external security audit recommends implementing Privileged Access Management (PAM) for Exchange Online
- Certain high-impact Exchange admin tasks should require approval before execution
- Tasks like 'New-TransportRule' and 'Set-Mailbox' should require approval

Question:
What does Microsoft 365 Privileged Access Management provide?
choices: Just-in-time activation of Azure AD admin roles (same as PIM)
Task-level approval workflow for specific admin actions within Microsoft 365 services
explanations: PIM provides role-level just-in-time access (activate the Global Admin role). PAM provides task-level approval (approve a specific admin action). They're different but complementary.

This option is correct. Microsoft 365 Privileged Access Management provides granular, task-level approval for specific admin actions within Microsoft 365 services. Instead of approving role activation (PIM), PAM requires approval for individual high-impact tasks. For example: an admin with the Exchange Administrator role must still request approval before running 'New-TransportRule'. An approver reviews and approves/denies the specific task. This provides an additional layer of control beyond role-level access.
MFA is an authentication mechanism, not a task-level approval workflow. MFA verifies identity; PAM controls what actions an authenticated admin can perform.
PAM manages admin task authorization, not communication encryption.
questions.tip: PIM vs PAM: PIM = role-level (can I activate Global Admin?). PAM = task-level (can I run New-TransportRule?). PAM workflow: admin requests access → approver reviews → approve/deny → time-limited permission to execute task. Supported services: Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, Teams. PAM policies: define which tasks need approval, who approves, time limits. Complementary: use PIM for role activation AND PAM for high-impact task approval. PAM requires: Microsoft 365 E5 or E5 Compliance.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your company uses Intune to manage devices
- The IT team wants to deploy a universal Windows Platform (UWP) app from the Microsoft Store to all managed Windows 11 devices
- The app is free and publicly available in the Microsoft Store
- It should install silently and be kept up to date

Question:
What is the recommended way to deploy a free Microsoft Store app through Intune?
choices: Tell users to install it from the Microsoft Store manually
Add the app using the 'Microsoft Store app (new)' type in Intune and assign as Required
Download the app package and deploy as a Win32 app
Use a PowerShell script to install the app via winget
explanations: Manual installation from the Store doesn't provide management, enforcement, or compliance reporting.

This option is correct. The 'Microsoft Store app (new)' type in Intune allows you to search for and add Store apps directly. Assign as Required for silent automatic installation. Intune handles deployment, installation status reporting, and automatic updates from the Microsoft Store. This is the simplest and recommended approach for Store apps — no packaging or manual download needed.
Downloading and wrapping as Win32 is unnecessarily complex when the Store app type handles everything automatically including updates.
Winget scripts can install apps but lack the management integration (status reporting, assignment management, automatic updates) that the native Store app type provides.
questions.tip: Microsoft Store app (new) in Intune: Search the Store directly from Intune → add app → assign. Benefits: no packaging needed, automatic updates from Store, silent install, status reporting. Assignment types: Required (auto-install), Available (Company Portal), Uninstall. Requirements: devices must have access to Microsoft Store service. Replaces: old Microsoft Store for Business integration (being retired). Works with: Windows 10/11 devices.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization uses Intune
- The IT team needs to manage Windows Defender Antivirus exclusions centrally
- Certain folders and file types must be excluded from real-time scanning for a business application
- Exclusions should be managed through Intune and apply to all targeted devices

Question:
Where do you configure Defender Antivirus exclusions in Intune?
choices: Endpoint security → Antivirus profile → Microsoft Defender Antivirus exclusions
explanations: Compliance policies evaluate whether antivirus is enabled, not configure antivirus exclusions.

This option is correct. Endpoint security → Antivirus profiles in Intune include a dedicated 'Microsoft Defender Antivirus exclusions' profile type. You can configure: file exclusions (specific file paths), folder exclusions (entire directories), file extension exclusions (.tmp, .log), and process exclusions (specific executables). These exclusions are deployed to targeted device groups and managed centrally.
Update ring settings manage Windows update delivery, not antivirus configuration.
App protection policies manage data protection in mobile apps. They don't configure Windows Defender Antivirus settings.
questions.tip: Defender Antivirus exclusions in Intune: Location: Endpoint security → Antivirus → create profile → Defender Antivirus exclusions. Exclusion types: Files (full path), Folders (directory path), File extensions (.ext), Processes (executable path). Best practices: minimize exclusions (each one reduces protection), document why each exclusion exists, review quarterly. Alternative locations: device configuration → Endpoint protection → Defender, or Settings Catalog. Caution: attackers target excluded folders — only exclude what's absolutely necessary.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization has Microsoft 365 E5
- The compliance team needs to create an Adaptive Protection policy
- Users identified as 'elevated risk' by Insider Risk Management should automatically receive stricter DLP policies
- As users' risk levels decrease, DLP policies should automatically relax

Question:
What does Adaptive Protection in Microsoft Purview do?
choices: Automatically updates antivirus signatures based on threat level
Dynamically adjusts DLP policy enforcement based on user risk levels from Insider Risk Management
Adapts firewall rules based on network threats
Changes password policies based on breach detection
explanations: Antivirus signature updates are handled by Microsoft Defender, not Adaptive Protection in Purview.

This option is correct. Adaptive Protection integrates Insider Risk Management with DLP. Users are dynamically classified into risk levels (elevated, moderate, minor) based on Insider Risk signals. DLP policies can reference these risk levels as conditions: elevated risk users get strict DLP (block sharing), moderate risk users get DLP with warnings, minor risk users get standard DLP. As user risk levels change, DLP enforcement automatically adjusts — no manual policy changes needed.
Firewall rule management is a network security function, not a Microsoft Purview feature.
Password policies are managed through Azure AD, not Adaptive Protection.
questions.tip: Adaptive Protection: Integration: Insider Risk Management → user risk levels → DLP policy conditions. Risk levels: Elevated, Moderate, Minor (assigned by Insider Risk). DLP conditions: 'User's insider risk level is elevated' → trigger strict DLP. Dynamic: risk level changes → DLP enforcement changes automatically. Example: user starts downloading unusual amounts of data → risk increases → DLP blocks external sharing → user stops risky behavior → risk decreases → DLP relaxes. Requires: Insider Risk Management + DLP (Microsoft 365 E5).

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your company uses Intune to manage macOS devices
- The IT team needs to configure FileVault disk encryption on all managed macOS devices
- Recovery keys must be stored in Intune for IT support to access if needed
- Users should be prompted to enable FileVault at next sign-out

Question:
Which Intune profile configures FileVault on macOS?
choices: Device compliance policy with encryption requirement
Endpoint security → Disk encryption → FileVault profile
explanations: Compliance policies check IF FileVault is enabled but don't configure or enable it. Compliance evaluates; endpoint security configures.

This option is correct. Endpoint security → Disk encryption in Intune provides a FileVault profile for macOS. Configure: enable FileVault, escrow recovery key to Intune, recovery key type (personal or institutional), prompt user at sign-out. When deployed, users are prompted to enable FileVault at their next sign-out. The personal recovery key is automatically escrowed to Intune, where IT admins can retrieve it if the user forgets their password.
Custom .mobileconfig profiles can configure FileVault but the built-in Intune FileVault profile is simpler and provides integrated recovery key management. Use the built-in option when available.
App protection policies manage data protection within mobile apps, not disk encryption on macOS.
questions.tip: FileVault management in Intune: Configure: Endpoint security → Disk encryption → macOS FileVault. Key settings: enable FileVault, escrow recovery key, prompt timing. Recovery key escrow: keys stored in Intune device properties. Key retrieval: Intune admin centre → Devices → macOS device → Recovery keys. Key rotation: can rotate recovery keys remotely. User experience: prompted at next sign-out to enable FileVault. Compliance: create separate compliance policy to check FileVault status.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization uses Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps
- The security team wants to control how users interact with specific sanctioned cloud apps in real-time
- When a user accesses Salesforce from an unmanaged device, they should be able to view data but not download files
- The control must work without installing any agent on the unmanaged device

Question:
Which Defender for Cloud Apps feature provides this real-time session control?
choices: Conditional Access App Control with session policies
explanations: Cloud Discovery identifies which cloud apps are in use (shadow IT). It doesn't control real-time user sessions.

This option is correct. Conditional Access App Control routes user sessions through Defender for Cloud Apps reverse proxy. Session policies then control what users can do in real-time: block downloads, block uploads, block cut/copy/paste, apply watermarks to displayed content, protect downloads with encryption. This works without any agent on the user's device because the session flows through the cloud proxy. Configure via Conditional Access → Session → 'Use Conditional Access App Control'.
File policies scan files already stored in connected cloud apps for sensitive content or sharing violations. They don't control real-time user sessions.
Activity policies trigger alerts based on user activities after they occur. They don't provide real-time session controls like blocking downloads.
questions.tip: Conditional Access App Control: How it works: Conditional Access routes session through Defender for Cloud Apps proxy. Session policy actions: Monitor only, Block download, Block upload, Block copy/paste, Apply watermark, Protect download. No agent needed: works via reverse proxy (browser-based). Configure: CA policy → session control → 'Use Conditional Access App Control'. Session policies: define granular controls per app per condition. Supported apps: Salesforce, Box, Dropbox, ServiceNow, and more (via SAML SSO).

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization uses Intune to manage Windows devices
- The IT team deploys several Win32 applications
- They need to understand the overall app installation success rate across the organization
- A report showing: total installations, successful, failed, and pending by app is needed

Question:
Where can the IT team find this app installation reporting?
choices: Azure AD admin centre → App registrations
Intune admin centre → Apps → Monitor → App install status
explanations: Azure AD App registrations shows cloud apps registered for authentication, not on-device application installations.

This option is correct. Intune admin centre → Apps → Monitor provides app installation status reports. For each deployed app, you can see: total targeted devices/users, installed (success), failed (with error codes), pending, and not installed. Click on an individual app for device-level detail showing which specific devices succeeded or failed. This provides the comprehensive installation reporting needed.
Microsoft 365 admin centre usage reports show cloud service usage (Teams calls, email volume) not device-level app installations.
Defender for Endpoint software inventory shows what's installed but doesn't track Intune deployment status (assigned, pending, failed, succeeded).
questions.tip: Intune app reporting: Per-app status: Apps → select app → Device install status / User install status. Monitor dashboard: Apps → Monitor → App install status (org-wide view). Per-device: Devices → select device → App install status (all apps on that device). Error codes: click failed installations to see specific error codes. Export: reports can be exported to CSV. Troubleshooting: failed installs → check IME log on device for details.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization manages both Windows and macOS devices with Intune
- The IT team wants to create a compliance policy that applies to BOTH Windows and macOS devices
- The policy should require: device encryption, antivirus, and minimum OS version

Question:
Can you create a single compliance policy that targets both Windows and macOS?
choices: Yes — create one cross-platform compliance policy
No — you must create separate compliance policies for each platform (Windows and macOS)
Yes — but only if the devices are co-managed
No — compliance policies only work for Windows
explanations: Intune compliance policies are platform-specific. You cannot create a single policy that spans multiple platforms.

This option is correct. Compliance policies in Intune are platform-specific — you must create separate policies for Windows, macOS, iOS, Android, etc. Each platform has different available compliance settings. Create a Windows compliance policy (BitLocker, Defender Antivirus, minimum Windows version) and a macOS compliance policy (FileVault, minimum macOS version) separately. Assign both to groups containing the respective device types.
Co-management doesn't enable cross-platform compliance policies. Co-management is specific to Windows devices managed by both MECM and Intune.
Compliance policies work for all supported platforms: Windows, macOS, iOS, iPadOS, Android, Linux.
questions.tip: Compliance policies are platform-specific: Windows → BitLocker, Defender, Windows version, TPM. macOS → FileVault, system integrity, macOS version. iOS → jailbreak detection, min OS version, passcode. Android → root detection, min OS version, encryption. Linux → custom compliance scripts. Cross-platform consistency: create matching policies per platform with equivalent settings. Use Azure AD dynamic device groups to target by platform automatically.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization uses Azure AD
- The IT team is configuring Self-Service Password Reset (SSPR)
- Requirements:
  - Users must register two authentication methods
  - Available methods: mobile phone, email, security questions, and Microsoft Authenticator
  - SSPR must work for all users including when they're off the corporate network

Question:
Where do you configure SSPR settings in Azure AD?
choices: Microsoft 365 admin centre → Settings → Password policy
Azure AD admin centre → Password reset → Properties, Authentication methods, Registration
Intune admin centre → Device compliance → Password settings
Exchange admin centre → Mail flow → Password reset
explanations: The Microsoft 365 admin centre has basic password policy settings (expiration, complexity) but doesn't provide the full SSPR configuration including authentication methods, registration requirements, and on-premises writeback.

This option is correct. Azure AD → Password reset provides comprehensive SSPR configuration: Properties → enable SSPR for all users or selected groups. Authentication methods → choose required methods and number of methods required (2). Registration → require users to register at sign-in, re-confirmation interval. Notifications → notify users and admins of password resets. On-premises integration → password writeback for hybrid environments.
Intune compliance policies check device password requirements (length, complexity) but don't configure Azure AD Self-Service Password Reset.
Exchange admin centre manages mail flow, not identity password management.
questions.tip: SSPR configuration: Enable: all users, selected groups, or none. Methods available: mobile phone, email, security questions, Authenticator app, FIDO2, office phone. Methods required: 1 or 2 (recommend 2 for security). Registration: force registration at next sign-in. Writeback: write passwords back to on-premises AD (requires Azure AD Connect). Combined registration: SSPR + MFA registration in a single experience. Licensing: SSPR requires Azure AD Premium P1+.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization uses Intune to manage Windows devices
- The IT team wants to implement Microsoft Defender for Endpoint on all managed devices
- Devices should be onboarded to Defender for Endpoint automatically when they enrol in Intune
- No manual onboarding scripts or packages should be needed

Question:
How do you enable automatic Defender for Endpoint onboarding for Intune-managed Windows devices?
choices: Run the onboarding script manually on each device
Enable the Microsoft Defender for Endpoint connector in Intune and create an endpoint detection and response (EDR) policy
Install Defender for Endpoint as a Win32 app
Configure Defender for Endpoint in Group Policy
explanations: Manual onboarding scripts don't scale and defeat the purpose of Intune's automated management. This is the legacy approach for non-Intune environments.

This option is correct. Enable the Intune-Defender for Endpoint service connector (Intune → Endpoint security → Microsoft Defender for Endpoint → Connection settings). Then create an EDR policy (Endpoint security → Endpoint detection and response) that deploys the onboarding configuration to devices. When a Windows device enrols in Intune, it automatically receives the EDR policy and onboards to Defender for Endpoint — no manual scripts needed.
Defender for Endpoint is built into Windows 10/11 — there's no separate app to install. The onboarding process activates the existing Defender sensors, not installs new software.
Group Policy can onboard devices but doesn't integrate with Intune's cloud management. For Intune-managed devices, the Intune connector is the recommended approach.
questions.tip: Defender for Endpoint + Intune integration: 1. Connect: Intune → Endpoint security → Microsoft Defender for Endpoint connector. 2. Enable: compliance integration, app protection evaluation. 3. Deploy: EDR policy → onboards devices automatically. 4. Compliance: include Defender risk score in compliance policy. Benefits: automatic onboarding, risk-based compliance, unified management. Defender risk score in compliance: if device risk exceeds threshold → non-compliant → CA blocks access.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
- Your organization uses Microsoft 365 E5
- The security team wants to simulate a credential harvesting phishing attack against all employees
- Users who enter their credentials in the simulated phishing page should be automatically enrolled in security awareness training
- The simulation results should show click rate, compromise rate, and training completion

Question:
Which Microsoft security feature provides phishing simulation and automated training assignment?
choices: Microsoft Defender for Endpoint automated investigation
Attack simulation training in Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Plan 2
explanations: Defender for Endpoint handles endpoint-level threats, not phishing simulations or security awareness training.

This option is correct. Attack simulation training in Defender for Office 365 Plan 2 allows you to create realistic phishing simulations (credential harvest, link in attachment, drive-by URL, OAuth consent). Users who 'fail' (click the link, enter credentials) are automatically assigned training modules.
